title: Kenya  shilling nudges higher on  intervention  talk
text:
NAIROBI, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling firmed slightly against the dollar on Friday, thanks to talk in the market that the Central Bank of Kenya was considering intervening to stem further falls, dealers said.

The central bank declined to comment.

At 1058 GMT, commercial banks posted the unit at 70.40/50 against the dollar compared with Thursday's close of 70.80/90.

Dealers said the unit was likely to stay stable at around 70.50/60 in the next few days.

"There was some material news which hit the market after it closed on Thursday. There was an attempt by the Central Bank to verbally intervene," said Chris Muiga, a senior dealer at Kenya Commercial Bank.

Traders said the regulator offered to sell dollars to stop the unit's slide. It had not, however, intervened in the end.

The shilling has been losing ground for the last week on heavy demand for greenbacks from importers.

"There is a feeling in the market that the Central Bank may not be happy with a weak shilling, so I think it will be anchored around 70.50/60," said Muiga.

James Ndegwa, an Imperial Bank trader, also said the unit was likely to stay stable.

title: Kenya shilling firms vs dlr, some banks cautious
text:
NAIROBI, May 22 (Reuters) - The Kenyan shilling <KES=> crept firmer against the dollar on Tuesday and some dealers said players were trading cautiously due to market concerns that the central bank could intervene to check further strengthening.   

At 1050 GMT, leading commercial banks traded the unit at 66.75/85 per dollar compared with 66.85/95 at the close of Friday's trade. It rose to 66.70/80 in earlier trade but demand by the telecommunications sector checked those gains.   

"People are looking at CBK ( Central Bank of Kenya) to give any communication whether they will intervene or not," said Duncan Kimani, a dealer at  Bank of Africa.

"People want to be on the safe side. No one wants to hold extreme positions."   

However, another trader said the central bank was unlikely to interfere with the market, although the local unit has strengthened to a four-year high.   

"I think CBK still believes the move is due to fundamentals," Peter Njuguna, a dealer at  Commercial Bank of Africa, said.   

Exporters have asked the central bank to check the rate as it was hurting their earnings.   

The central bank has said it would only intervene if it detected speculation. Traders said the next psychological barrier was the 66.50 level.

title: Intervention  props Uganda, Tanzania shillings
text:
NAIROBI, May 31 (Reuters) - The Kenya shilling <KES=> held steady against the dollar, while the Tanzanian <TZS=> and Ugandan <UGX=> currencies had to be propped up by intervention in the week to Wednesday, dealers said.  

KENYA

The Kenya shilling held steady against the dollar in the week to Wednesday. At 1125 GMT the shilling traded at 72.05/25 to the dollar, compared with last Wednesday's close of 72.00/10.  

The shilling initially strengthened to touch 71.60/80 to the dollar as banks sold off the U.S. currency, then it weakened to touch 72.50/60 to the dollar, undermined by importers demand.  

"It has been quite volatile. We experienced a bit of turbulence," said Peter Njuguna, of Commercial Bank of Africa.  

The shilling has since regained ground, lifted by dollar inflows and as banks took profits, dealers said.  

"Initially people took long positions, anticipating end month demand, but as we came into this week there was not much demand and we've seen interbank players sell into the market," said a dealer at Barclays Bank.  

Dealers said they expect the shilling to trade in the 71.75-72.60 range against the dollar in coming days, with a bias for it to hover around 72.00.  

UGANDA  

The Ugandan shilling weakened against the dollar, undermined by increased dollar demand from banks and corporate clients, but central bank intervention prevented further losses.  

At 1100 GMT commercial banks quoted the shilling at 1,848/1,853 to the dollar, compared with 1,835/1,840 at last Wednesday's close.  

"We have seen the shilling slide lower against the dollar due to increased corporate demand mainly from the telecommunication sector and the interbank market," Catherine Kijjaggulwi, a dealer at Barclays Bank, said.  

Dealers said the central bank intervened on Monday and Wednesday, putting brakes on the shilling's weakening.  

"The central bank has intervened on the sale side mainly to smoothen out depreciation of the shilling," said David Bagambe, chief dealer at DFCU Bank.  

Dealers forecast the shilling will continue to depreciate in the absence of central bank intervention to close the week at 1,855 levels.  

"Anticipated end-month inflows are too weak to meet the surge in dollar demand in the market. Unless the central bank intervenes with substantial amounts to prop the shilling, the market will continue to see it slide," Bagambe said.  

TANZANIA  

The Tanzania shilling <TZS=> firmed marginally against the dollar in the week to Wednesday, amid increased demand from the telecoms and energy sectors, buoyed by central bank intervention.  

At 0935 GMT the local unit traded at 1,247/1,257 to the dollar, compared with last Wednesday's close of 1,250/1,258, dealers said.  

During the week, the shilling weakened to levels of 1,255/1,265, but central Bank of Tanzania (BOT) came to the market to sell the dollar at 1,250 shillings.  

"There was high demand for the dollar, especially from the telecoms and the oil sector. The demand could not match the supply," said Rose Mollel, a senior dealer at CRDB Bank.  

Dealers said that BOT intervened three times during the week.  

"This has been the result of central bank coming to the market and selling dollars at very low prices from where the market was," said Samwuel Marco, a dealer at Stanbic Bank.  

Dealers said they expect the shilling to continue gaining against the dollar, boosted by BOT's continued presence in the market, and by corporate clients selling dollars to meet their shilling-denominated end-month payments.

title: East African  currencies  mixed vs dlr, Tanzanian up
text:
NAIROBI, April 12 (Reuters) - East African currencies traded mixed against the U.S. dollar in the week to Wednesday, traders said.  

The Kenyan and Ugandan units were marginally weaker while the Tanzanian shilling strengthened on the back of central bank intervention.  

KENYA

The Kenya shilling <KES=> was slightly weaker versus the dollar but traders expect it to stay in a range in coming days.  

At 1000 GMT, leading commercial banks posted the currency at 71.05/71.25 compared with 71.00/71.20 at close of trading last Wednesday.  

The unit weakened to a low of 71.80/90 in early Tuesday's trade but clawed back its losses on some agricultural export supplies.  

"Demand and supply are kind of matching up," said Moses Kiboi, a senior dealer at Citibank, predicting a 71.00 - 71.80 range. "Unless we get any new factors, there is no reason for it to change out of its comfort zone."  

A Barclays Bank dealer said the local unit had weakened from dwindling inflows from tourism and horticulture industries.  

"The shilling has been weakening gradually because of importer demand and also we are seeing reduced flows from the tourism and horticulture sectors," the Barclays dealer said.  

UGANDA  

The Ugandan shilling <UGX=> eased against the greenback despite light corporate demand matching minimal U.S. dollar inflows, dealers said.  

Leading commercial banks quoted the local unit at 1,822/1,828 per dollar compared to last week's close of 1,825/1,830.  

"We have seen some inflows from traditional sources like the non-governmental organisations and the tourism sector which have been matched by the light corporate demand," said Moses Elungat, head of trading at Barclays Bank.  

The shilling is expected to come under pressure as corporate players step up demand.  

"The shilling could remain under pressure as long as the current level of demand is sustained," another dealer said.  

"However, if the inflows outstrip dollar demand, then the shilling will ease off to levels of 1,825/1,830 after the Easter holidays this weekend."  

TANZANIA  

The Tanzania shilling <TZS=> appreciated slightly against the dollar on the back of dollar sales by the central bank amid weakening demand for greenbacks by oil importers, dealers said.  

Banks posted the unit at 1,222/1,227 shillings to a greenback compared with 1,225/1,230 at last Wednesday's close.  

"We saw Bank of Tanzania in the market selling dollars. This calmed the market a bit," said Alex Ngusaru, treasurer at Citibank. "They may sell more since they have enough foreign reserves. I don't see why they should not come in."  

Another dealer said the market received less dollar demand by oil importers as rains in the country have helped raise the water levels in hydroelectric dams.  

Tanzanian electricity authorities were earlier this year forced to cut supply by up to 12 hours per day due to a severe drought that had hit the region.  

Many people in the country were compelled to purchase fuel-run generators to provide power.  

Dealers anticipate more central bank intervention should the shilling come under pressure, but they also expect banks to unwind long dollar positions.  

"We are seeing some tightness in shilling liquidity and due to that, we might see banks offloading positions they hold which means an appreciation of the shilling in the short term," said Aziz Chacha, head of market making at Barclays Bank Tanzania.

title: Kenya anti-graft body says probed c.bank governor
text:
NAIROBI, March 7 (Reuters) - The Kenya anti-corruption agency said on Tuesday it had investigated central bank governor Andrew Mullei over corruption allegations and forwarded its recommendations to the attorney general for action.  

"We did receive some complaints, allegations, which we did investigate some time back," Nicholas Simani, the spokesman of the Kenya Anti-Corruption Commission (KACC) told Reuters.  

"We came up with specific recommendations which we forwarded to the attorney general for appropriate action," he added but refused to divulge details of the recommendations.  

Kenya's tabloids have repeatedly carried stories accusing Mullei of nepotism and corruption at the central bank.  

The Standard, one of Kenya's leading newspapers, reported on Tuesday that the Ministry of Finance had asked KACC to investigate Mullei over allegations of corruption.  

There was no immediate comment from the Ministry of Finance or the governor's office.  

The Standard said KACC had received the letter from the Ministry of Finance on Feb. 27 and had not acted on it. But Simani said KACC had completed its own investigations on the governor on Feb 23.  

The anti-graft body has no powers to prosecute which are vested in the office of the attorney general.  

The allegations of corruption in the central bank are the latest to rock President Mwai Kibaki's government whose image has suffered badly after three senior ministers resigned over graft.  

The finance, energy and education ministers resigned last month after their names were linked to two graft scandals in which millions of state funds were corruptly paid out.  

Mullei, who has strongly rejected recent pressure by manufacturers and exporters to intervene in the currency market to weaken the strong Kenya shilling, has previously faced allegations of wrongdoing over a banknotes printing tender.  

He denied any wrongdoing over the tender which was later awarded to Britain's De La Rue Currency.  

Mullei was appointed by Kibaki in March 2003. As the governor, he enjoys security of tenure. Under Kenyan laws, the governor can be sacked if convicted of dishonesty or fraud or upon the recommendations of a tribunal appointed by the president to investigate him.

title: Strong Kenya  currency  to slash tea farmers earnings
text:
NAIROBI, Feb 6 (Reuters) - Kenyan tea farmers could lose 10 percent of their earnings if the local shilling <KES=> keeps its strong tone against the dollar, a key agency grouping small-scale tea producers said on Monday.  

The Kenyan shilling has been trading at a 2-1/2 year high against the dollar in the last few days and the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) Governor Andrew Mullei has said he would not intervene to influence the value of the currency.  

"Ours is an appeal to the government to do something about it because what will happen at the end of the year is that farmers will loose 10 percent of their income," David Kimani, the finance director at the Kenya Tea Development Agency (KTDA) told reporters.  

"We are talking about a balance that ensures we exporters survive and importers too, survive."  

At 1400 GMT, the shilling traded at 71.00/20 shillings to a dollar.  

Kenya is one of the world's biggest exporters of black tea earning the east African country about 43 billion Kenya shillings ($604.8 million) annually.  

"The current exchange rates are literally killing the industry. I don't know how much longer we can operate at the shilling's current rate," Lerionka Tiampati, KTDA's managing director said.  

The agency, which accounts for over 60 percent of Kenya's annual tea production, said a severe drought in the country had affected production with some regions picking green leaf only three days in a week instead of six days.  

Industry players expect that poor rains in the last three years will slash the country's production by about 30 percent.  

Tea was once known as Kenya's green gold, but oversupply, spiralling production costs, stagnant prices, competition from emerging markets growing lower quality but cheaper tea and the trend towards coffee have hit the industry hard.

title: UPDATE 1- Kenya  cenbank won't  intervene  over shilling
text:

NAIVASHA, Kenya, Feb 3 (Reuters) - Kenya's Central Bank will not intervene in local currency markets despite the current strength of the shilling against the U.S. dollar, governor Andrew Mullei said on Friday.  

"The CBK shall not take measures that influence the exchange position of exchange rate," he told reporters in the town of Naivasha, north of Nairobi, after opening a seminar.  

Mullei said there was no justification for intervention.  

"The bank can only intervene if we see that the exchange rate is being influenced by speculative attacks which is not currently the case," he said.  

"Currently the exchange rate is influenced by growth in the supply and limited demand for (foreign) currency in Kenya."  

Exporters say the strong shilling, trading around a 2-1/2 year high at 71.30/58 against the dollar, is seriously harming them. But Mullei sought to reassure them relief would come eventually.  

"In due course we shall see that the shilling exchange rate conforms to what might be of use to exporters," he said, adding that intervention to inject demand for foreign exchange would lead to inflationary pressure.  

"The CBK acts say that the Bank ensures that inflation is kept under control and thus we can't take action that perpetuates inflation," he added.

title: ANALYSIS-No let up in Kenya shilling rally despite concerns
text:
NAIROBI, Sept 19 (Reuters) - The Kenya shilling is expected to continue its advance against the dollar in the short term and could touch the key 73/dollar level this week, but may struggle to break higher, currency analysts said on Monday.  

The shilling has gained nearly 6.8 percent so far this year, triggering complaints from local manufacturers and other exporters who say it has made their products uncompetitive.  

The shilling on Monday rose to a fresh five-and-a-half month high of 73.25/45.  

After pushing through a series of resistance levels in quick succession in the last few weeks, analysts say the 73.00 level is at hand.  

"All the flows that we have been seeing coming in from the export sector and the limited demand that we have been seeing from, especially the energy sector, have served to drive the shilling higher and higher," said Kihara Maina, the treasurer at Barclay Bank.  

"We are looking at touching the year high because the market is seeing it is within sight," he said, referring to the 73.10 level that was the highest the shilling has been in the past 12 months.  

But dealers said they expect the 73 level to provide strong resistance for the shilling.  

"We may see some importers taking advantage of these low levels to take up forwards and cover their requirements through to the end of the year," said Timothy Kabiru, treasurer at the Cooperative Bank of Kenya.  

CURRENT ACCOUNT  

Kenya's current account deficit widened by $838 million in the 12 months to May 2005, in part due to high global oil prices and increased imports of machinery and transport equipment, suggesting the local currency should have come under pressure.  

However, heavy inflows particularly from tea, horticulture and coffee exporters, combined with receipts from a booming tourism sector, have lent strong support for the shilling.  

Even more significant are relatively high domestic interest rates. The average yield on benchmark 91-day treasury bill stood at 8.5 percent at the last auction on Thursday compared with 2.9 percent posted the same time last year.  

"Obviously people are keen to get the shilling yield at rates of about eight and a half percent as opposed to the dollar at about three and a half percent," Barclay's Maina said.  

The high rates also have discouraged importers, especially oil companies, from hedging themselves in the forward market.  

While the shilling's rally has led many importers to stay on the sidelines, a recent comment by Central Bank governor Andrew Mullei that the gains reflected the country's improved economic performance was providing further support.  

"Comments like the one that the central bank has issued that this is a reflection of the economy and things like that, that has given an impetus to the shilling," said Jeremiah Kendagor, the head of foreign exchange at Kenya Commercial Bank.  

INTERVENTION

Mullei, who has rejected calls to intervene in the market to weaken the shilling, said 10 days ago that the exchange rate reflected the brisk growth in the domestic economy and investor optimism which was attracting strong foreign inflows.  

The Kenyan economy expanded by 4.3 percent in 2004 compared with 2.8 percent in 2003. A survey by a leading local research firm on business confidence released last week showed that most chief executives were bullish on the economy's prospects.  

"What you see now with the shilling is a by-product of a very rapidly growing economy. Because if the economy was declining in performance, we would be seeing the exchange rate depreciating," Mullei told reporters at a function where he released the central bank's monetary policy on Sept. 9.  

The governor said he expected to see the shilling weaken as demand for imports to support the growing econonomy increases.  

"I see the reversal of the exchange rate of the shilling torwards either stability or depreciation."

title: Traders predict a weaker path for Kenyan shilling.
text:
NAIROBI, April 1 (Reuters) - The Kenya shilling  is expected to fall to a range of 76.00-77.50 to the dollar in the short-term after verbal intervention by the central bank and on an anticipated rise in importer demand, analysts said on Friday.    

 The shilling has risen steadily in recent months, gaining 10 percent since mid-December when it started its latest rally.    

 It rose to a 21-month high of 72.90/73.10 on March 21, and the central bank, worried about Kenya's competitiveness, warned that it would intervene to stem any speculation on the shilling.    

 Dealers said the shilling's gains were overdone and the central bank's comments were the trigger that was needed to reverse the shilling's path.    

 The unit closed on Thursday at 74.60/80 to the dollar.    

 "I think the move down to 73.00 was overdone. It was only a matter of time before it reversed. These levels were not sustainable at the end of the day," said Robert Otieno, the treasurer at Stanbic Bank.    

 Experts say the local unit has been well-supported by dollar receipts from the farm and tourism sectors, strong inflows from non-governmental organisations and investors seeking to purchase high-yield shilling-denominated government bonds.    

 On the other hand, dollar demand has been severely subdued, with most importers, especially the key oil companies, already hedged and staying on the sidelines as the shilling appreciated.    

 But dealers and analysts said the shilling's previous pattern suggests that the unit is headed lower and importers are just about to return to the market.    

 NET IMPORT ECONOMY    

 "The shilling is going to see some weakness because cyclically we are about due for that kind of weakening and even structurally, with a net import economy, you would generally tend to have a weaker currency," said Kihara Maina, the treasurer at Barclays Bank of Kenya. "I see a consolidation around the 76, the 77 level."    

 OIL PRICES    

 Analysts said higher oil prices are also expected to exert pressure on the local unit. Oil surged back above $55 a barrel on Thursday and analysts said prices could rise further.    

 "The $50 a barrel is still a lot for an oil-importing country like Kenya and that suggests that it is unlikely that the shilling would be able to hold on to its strengths indefinitely," Razia Khan, Standard Chartered Bank's chief Africa economist.    

 "Despite the near-term strength in the shilling we think 77.50 in a few weeks time is still a possibility and then gradually weakening beyond that," she told Reuters from London.    

 Although higher interest rates - at 8.67 percent - were a key factor supporting the shilling, an aggressive interest rate hike in the U.S. could pressure the Kenyan unit, analysts said.    

 "Kenyan interest rates would have to be somewhat higher with the Fed continuing to hike rates so that yields attraction will remain in place," Khan said.    

 The market had its eyes fixed on the outcome of a two-week visit by a mission from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) currently in the country to review its programme.    

 "I think obviously people are waiting to see what happens when the current negotiations between the...IMF, who are around, and the government to see whether they are releasing aid to Kenya," Otieno said.

title: Kenyan shilling falls after c.bank comments.
text:
NAIROBI, March 29 (Reuters) - The Kenyan shilling
weakened against the dollar in early trade on Tuesday as the
market reacted to comments by the central bank that it would
intervene to stop any speculation in the market, dealers said.
    At 0745 GMT, leading commercial banks were quoting the
shilling at 74.60/80 to the dollar, compared to Thursday's close
of 73.25/45.
    Central Bank Governor Andrew Mullei said late on Thursday
that the bank would take "corrective action" if the firming
shilling faced speculative pressures and added that he expected
the unit to weaken in due course as demand for foreign exchange
increases.
    The news came after the local currency market had closed and
players only reacted to it on Tuesday because the markets
remained closed on Friday and Monday for Easter holidays.
  


    "It's largely on the back of central bank's comment that
they were prepared to take corrective action on the shilling,
and basically that happened after that market closed," said
Anthony Kirui, the head of market making at Barclays Bank.
 
    "What we're seeing today is people wishing to cover their
short positions."
    The shilling has been on an upward trend in recent weeks and
rallied to a 21-month high of 72.90/73.10 to the dollar last
week, prompted by a huge dollar sell-off by banks.
    The central bank said the shilling had been boosted by
  

increased demand for shilling-denominated government bonds,  

coupled with subdued demand for dollars at a time when dollar  

inflows have been heavy.  

But some analysts said the shilling's recent gains were  

overdone and feared that they could undermine the  

competitiveness of Kenya's export sector.  

"It is the market reaction to the central bank sentiment  

that they will intervene in the market. The market took a cue  

from that and decided to intervene themselves," said Jeremiah  

Kendagor, a senior dealer at Kenya Commercial Bank.  

"We've seen interbank players come into the market to buy  

dollars. We've also seen importers come into the market as well  

and buy dollars to meet their obligations," Kirui said, adding  

that he expected the shilling to remain volatile for the rest of  

the day.

title: Kenya shilling down slightly as dollar demand rises.
text:
NAIROBI, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The Kenyan shilling weakened marginally against the dollar on Friday, as month-end demand started to kick in, traders said.  

At 0845 GMT, leading commercial banks in Nairobi posted the rate as 81.30/50 against the dollar, down slightly from the opening of 81.30/45.  

"Month-end demand will really kick in from next week. We have been seeing some increase from corporates. That tells me that a lot of them are getting ready to meet their (month-end) obligations," said Bryan Muigai, a trader at Standard Chartered Bank.  

Kenya's currency market has been subdued in the last few months, with dealers predicting the shilling would remain in a tight range of 80.90/81.50 in the short term, barring any new market-moving news.  

Kenya's central bank Governor Andrew Mullei, who intervened in the market earlier this year to combat sharp drops in the shilling, said on Tuesday he was comfortable with the current exchange rate.  

He told Reuters that supply and demand were evenly matched and that fundamentals indicated the rate was where it should be.

title: Kenyan shilling flat vs dlr after c.bank acts.
text:
NAIROBI, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The Kenyan shilling  was little changed against the U.S. dollar on Friday after the central bank again sold the greenback to prop up the local currency, traders said.    

 At 0855 GMT, leading commercial banks posted the shilling at 80.07/80.27 against the U.S. currency, barely changed from Thursday's 80.10/80.30 close.    

 Dealers said the shilling was under pressure from oil importers and distributors seeking U.S. currency to pay for purchases of refined products, with world petroleum prices near historic highs.    

 Dollar demand fuelled by high oil import bills helped push the shilling to historic lows of 83.25/45 last month.    

 Other pressure this week came from a dearth of foreign currency receipts from the tea sector, with output and exports depressed by unfavourable weather, said Kennedy Butiko of Bank of Africa Kenya.    

 On August 26 the central bank disclosed it had intervened the prop up the shilling, blaming its rapid slide on speculation by some market players and saying a rate weaker than 79 shillings could not be explained by fundamentals.    

 The bank sold dolllars into the market again on Friday. A bank official declined to disclosed the amounts involved.    

 Dealers said the overall outlook for the shilling was still unsettled, amid jitters over the intentions of international lenders and donors who help fund the government's budget and development proghrammes.    

 "The underlying sentiment on the shilling's future direction is uncertainty over donor policy," said Moses Kiboi of Citibank.    

 The shilling took a knock in July when the European Union disclosed it had postponed a decision on an aid package Kenya needs to finance its budget.    

 The move, a fresh sign of donor impatience with the government's faltering anti-corruption campaign, fuelled fears that donors were considering suspending aid the east African country desperately needs to escape from poverty.    

 The EU and other top international donors warned Kenya earlier this year that it risked losing vital funding, saying corruption still appeared to be at the heart of government despite President Mwai Kibaki's promises to stamp it out.

title: Kenya  c.bank says  intervenes  to sell dollars.
text:
NAIROBI, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Kenya's central bank sold dollars on the foreign exchange market on Friday, an official at the bank said, confirming the second such intervention by the regulator in support of the shilling in eight days.   

"We have been in the market to sell dollars. We cannot confirm the amounts," the official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters. The last known intervention by the bank came on August 26 when the bank disclosed it had acted to prop up the shilling.

title: UPDATE 2-Kenya ready to end shilling speculation-c.bank.
text:
NAIROBI, Aug 27 (Reuters) - Kenya's central bank, which intervened this week to stem a slide in the shilling, remains ready to ensure an end to speculation in the currency and some risk takers "stand to lose", the bank's governor said on Friday.   

Andrew Mullei told a news conference that a fall in the currency below 79 to the U.S. dollar - the shilling actually hit a historic low of 83.25/45 on Wednesday - could not be explained by fundamentals.   

"The central bank stands ready to make sure the speculative activity is brought to an end. Some risk takers stand to lose," Mullei said, speaking after the market closed.   

"We are moving very cautiously because it is not the intention of the central bank to control the level of the    


 
 exchange rate....The purpose of us going to the market is to
 protect the interests of importers."
   The bank intervened on Thursday to prop up the currency,
   

which has fallen steadily from around 79.60 three months ago. It was unchanged in early dealings at 81.00/20 on Friday, later firming to 80.86/81.06.   

The slide has been blamed on several factors including hints by donors that they might pull aid out of Kenya over graft allegations and high global oil prices.   

"The exchange rate beyond 79 cannot be explained by fundamentals," Mullei said. "If it were an excess of demand compared to supply (of dollars) we would not have proceeded to the market to intervene."   

"It is not our intention to cause losses for any players in the market. But if we warn some players are overplaying, but you don't see a reaction then you have to become mechanical (intervene)."   

DONOR WARNINGS   

The shilling began coming under heavy pressure in July when the European Union (EU) said it had postponed a decision on an aid package Kenya needs to finance its budget.   

The EU deferred consideration of 125 million euros in budget support until September or October, although it said longer-term development aid would continue.   

The move was a fresh sign of donor impatience with the government's faltering anti-corruption campaign and fuelled fears that donors were considering suspending aid the east African country desperately needs to escape from poverty.   

The EU and other top international donors warned Kenya earlier in July that it risked losing vital funding, saying corruption still appeared to be at the heart of government despite President Mwai Kibaki's promises to stamp it out.   

Kenya's 2004/05 (July/June) budget depends heavily on aid. Presenting the budget last month, Finance Minister David Mwiraria said 50.7 billion shillings ($633 million), or 11.5 percent of total spending, would be donor-funded.   

But Mullei said even if donors withheld promised funds, the government had enough in reserve to maintain a stable shilling.   

"Even if our development partners delay until the end of the year, the effect of that delay would not affect the reserves needed to keep the exchange rate stable," he said.   

He said key indicators over the last two years, particularly inflation, all showed Kenya's economy was on the right track.   

"To keep inflation below three percent, for a developing country running a budget deficit, is really a success. Kenya's performance on that score is exemplary," he said.   

"This is steady progress for the Kenyan economy. The thing is working, and working in the way that it should be working."

title: Kenya  shilling steady vs dlr after c.bank  intervention .

title: Emerging  FX -Turbulence subsides in forint, zloty.
text:
LONDON, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint and Polish zloty traded calmer on Thursday after both were whipped around in the previous session on domestic political and economic developments.  

The Kenyan shilling firmed after the central bank was seen entering the market to prop it up after sharp losses against the dollar.  

Hungary's ruling Socialist party selected the charismatic millionaire Ferenc Gyurcsany to be the country's new Prime Minister after he defeated party stalwart Peter Kiss at the party's special congress on Wednesday. After an initial move lower the forint steadied at around 249 per euro . Analysts said the market would probably give Gyurcsany the benefit of the doubt until his policy intentions became clearer.  

"Gyurcsany is an unknown and the fact he's an ex-businessman who benefited from early 90s privatisations doesn't necessarily make him a market friendly figure," said Koon Chow, emerging markets strategist at CSFB.  

"I'm still mindful of the Socialist party's low popularity and fearful of further desperate measures they might take to shore that up," he added.  

By 0935 GMT, the forint was flat from late Wednesday levels at 249.20 to the euro.  

Investors have been encouraged by early signs of continuity on budget policy, with a close aide of Gyurcsany's saying that Finance Minister Tibor Draskovics, seen as a key guardian of the fiscal consolidation process in Hungary, would keep his post.  

Chow said the forint's high carry - benchmark interest rates are at 11 percent - was also likely to keep the currency well supported in any dips.  

The Polish zloty jumped to two week highs around 4.3830 against the euro on Wednesday after the central bank surprised the market with a bigger-than-expected 50 basis point rate hike, taking key rates to 6.5 percent. The currency handed back its gains later on.  

"The zloty had gone up after the rate hike but then someone had an order to buy a large amount of euro/polish and that squeezed a few people out the other way," said one London bank trader.  

The market retained its weaker bias on Thursday and Chow at CSFB said that could reflect part of a broader trend across the region.  

"Technical analysts have been warning for the past three weeks that the strength of central European currencies against the euro is fading and we could be going through a period of weakness. That fits in with the already large positioning in the market."   


The zloty traded at 4.4469 per euro  from 4.4349 and at 3.6846 to the
dollar        from 3.6720.
  

KENYA INTERVENES TO DEFEND SHILLING  

The Kenyan shilling rose sharply off record lows around 83.25/45 against the dollar hit on Wednesday after dealers reported the central bank intervening in the market to defend the currency.  

The central bank said in a statement it was taking steps to stabilise the dollar/shilling rate, adding that the shilling's rapid weakening had been caused by speculative pressure applied by domestic players.  

Dealers have blamed shilling weakness on a variety of factors, including growing corruption allegations in government which have led to fears donors may desert the country and high global oil prices.  

The shilling bounced to 81 per dollar .  

Softer-than-expected South African July producer prices (PPI) offered further vindication for the central bank's shock 50 basis point rate cut earlier this month.  

July PPI came in at an annual rate of 0.7 percent, below a Reuters poll consensus forecast of 1.3 percent.  

The rand was little moved on the data, holding steady around 6.67 to the dollar .

title: Kenya  shilling rises on c.bank  intervention .
text:
NAIROBI, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The Kenya shilling rose sharply against the U.S. dollar on Thursday after the central bank sold the greenback to reverse a rapid depreciation by the local currency, traders said.  

The shilling dropped below the key psychological level of 81 versus the dollar on Friday, and reached a fresh historic low of 83.25/45 shillings per dollar in early trading on Wednesday.  

On Thursday the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) entered the market and sold dollars, sending the local unit racing up to 80.90/81.10 by 0745 GMT, after Wednesday's close of 82.40/60.  

"The market has been a beehive of activity this morning," said Citibank dealer Moses Kiboi. "We've seen people selling off long dollar positions and the shilling has appreciated rapidly." CBK Governor Andrew Mullei said the central bank, as well as importers of goods and services, were concerned by the recent rapid fall in the price of the local currency.  

"To calm the local foreign exchange market, the Central Bank has taken steps to stabilise the Kenya shilling exchange rate and ensure that it reflects the true market value of the shilling," he said in a statement issued on Thursday morning.  

"The major cause of the recent rapid weakening of the shilling against the U.S. dollar has been the intensity of speculative activities by some local market players," he added.  

Traders in Nairobi said the central bank sold dollars on Thursday and sent the shilling climbing against the greenback.  

"Clients had been complaining that there was no liquidity and traders had been pushing up the rate saying (dollar) inflows could not match demand," one trader at a major bank said.  

The recent slide by the shilling, which has fallen from around 79.60 three months ago, has been blamed on several factors including hints by donors that they might pull aid out of Kenya over graft allegations and high global oil prices.

title: UPDATE 1- Kenya  c.bank  intervenes  to prop shilling-traders.
text:
NAIROBI, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Kenya's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Thursday, selling dollars to prop the recently weak shilling, traders said.    

Central bank governor Andrew Mullei issued a brief statement saying the bank had acted to stabilise the shilling following a rapid decline against the U.S. dollar.    

 However, the brief statement did not specify what steps the bank had taken.    

 "The central bank was in the market selling dollars this morning. Clients had been complaining that there was no liquidity and traders had been pushing up the rate saying (dollar) inflows could not match demand," a trader at a major bank said.    

 The central bank's statement said it, as well as importers of goods and services, was concerned by the shilling's rapid weakening in recent days.    

 "To calm the local foreign exchange market, the Central Bank has taken steps to stabilise the Kenya shilling exchange rate and ensure that it reflects the true market value of the shilling," Mullei's statement said.    

 "The major cause of the recent rapid weakening of the shilling against the U.S. dollar has been the intensity of speculative activities by some local market players," he added.    

 The shilling traded on Thursday at 80.90/81.10 against the U.S. currency, dealers said, up from a fresh historic low of 83.25/45 shillings hit in early trade on Wednesday. The currency recovered later on Wednesday to about 82.80/83.00.    

 The recent slide by the shilling, which has fallen from around 79.60 three months ago, has been blamed on several factors including hints by donors that they might pull aid out of Kenya over graft allegations and high global oil prices.

title: Kenyan shilling eases slightly on dollar demand.
text:
NAIROBI, Aug 19 (Reuters) - The Kenyan shilling
weakened marginally against the dollar on Thursday as importers
from the agriculture, energy and manufacturing sectors bought
the U.S. currency to meet end of month bills, trader said.
    At 0950 GMT, leading commercial banks posted the shilling at
80.95/81.05 against the greenback compared with Wednesday's
close of 80.80/81.00.
    However, the threat of central bank intervention after the
shilling hit historic lows was expected to keep the local unit
at around the 80.80/81.00 level, dealer said.
    "There's some importer demand from maize, energy, even some
manufacturing companies," said Kennedy Butiko of Bank of Africa
Kenya.
    "We're not seeing (the shilling) go beyond 81.00 on fears of
CBK (Central Bank of Kenya) intervention. Dealers are cautious
about pushing it beyond that level," he added.
    CBK Governor Andre Mullei late on Tuesday blamed the
shilling's recent fall to historic lows on speculation by
commercial banks.
   


 He added that the bank would act to ensure the
shilling was stable and purely determined by demand and supply.
 
    A Barclays Bank dealer said importers had suspended their
orders but were forced to buy dollars as the end of month looms.
    "Importers believed at 81.00 the shilling (weakness) was
overdone and were looking for a reversal," he said.
    Butiko added: "They were forced to make a decision to buy,
especially the oil sector."
    Currency dealers have blamed a number of factors on the
   

shilling's fall from donor threats to halt aid to Kenya because   

of rising cases of corruption and high global oil prices to   

pending importer demand estimated at $50 million for four   

million 90-kg bags of maize.

title: Ugandan, Tanzanian shillings rise, Kenyan perks up.
text:
NAIROBI, Aug 18 (Reuters) - The Uganda        and Tanzania
  shillings rose in the week to Wednesday against the
dollar while the Kenya shilling  began reversing a slide
to historic lows as the country's central bank warned it might
step in to stabilise the currency.
     Kenya's central bank governor Andrew Mullei late on Tuesday
blamed the local unit's recent fall on speculation by commercial
banks. He added the central bank would act to ensure the
shilling rate is stable and purely determined by supply and
demand.
 
    The shilling raced to 80.60/80 to the dollar at Wednesday's
open from 80.95/81.15 at Tuesday's close.
    But the local unit gave up some of those gains on the back
of some light corporate dollar demand. At 1000 GMT it was quoted
at 80.75/95 to the dollar, dealers said.
    "Nobody wants to take chances after the CBK (the Central
Bank of Kenya) threatened to intervene," said Moses Kiboi, a
senior dealer at Citibank.
  

Currency dealers of late have blamed the shilling's fall on
a number of factors including pending importer demand estimated
at $50 million for 4 million 90-kg bags of maize.
    Political concerns, donor threats to pull aid from Kenya due
to rising cases of corruption and high global oil prices have
kept downward pressure on the shilling as well.
    Meanwhile, the Tanzania shilling kept strengthening against
  

the dollar, buoyed by sustained dollar sales by the Bank of  

Tanzania (BoT) and agricultural exports which dealers expect to  

continue in coming weeks.  

The shilling's exchange rate stood at 1,080/1,084 shillings  

per dollar compared to 1,084/1,087 shillings at Wednesday's  

close of trading.  

"We have seen the shilling appreciating on a daily basis.  

There are a lot of supplies from the agricultural sector and at  

the same time, the central bank is selling," Christopher Mutasa,  

treasury manager at the African Banking Corporation said.   


 
    "It's really going to appreciate if central bank continue
selling and with more exporters in the market."
    Dealers said there was little corporate demand. Some
surmised the central bank might be selling dollars to reach a
target of shilling requirements by the end of the quarter.
    "We don't feel they will be out of the market soon," said
  

Marco Samwel, a dealer at Stanbic Bank. "If they were close to  

their target, they would not have allowed the shilling to  

strengthen to this point."   


 
    In Uganda, the shilling gained strength against the dollar
over the week due to low corporate demand for the greenback.
    At 1000 GMT leading commercial banks were quoting the local
unit at 1,698/1,700 shillings per U.S. dollar, compared to
1,725/1,745 shillings a week ago.
    "The shilling has continued to rally ... basically on the
  

back of absence of corporate dollar demand and significant  

inflows of dollars from non-governmental organisations and  

projects," said Moses Elungat, head of trading at Barclays.   


 
    Traders said intervention earlier in the week by the central
Bank of Uganda (BoU) had also boosted the shilling.
    "The central bank sterilised the market on Monday by
intervening on the sale side. This triggered off the rally,"
said Sophie Achak, a trader at Stanbic bank.
    BoU's "sterilisation" funds are dollars, largely for
development projects, that it receives from international donors
and needs to convert into the local currency.
    Without improved demand for the U.S. currency from corporate
  

clients, traders said they expected the shilling to stabilise at  

levels of around 1,690/1,700 in the days ahead.  

(Additional reporting by Daniel Wallis in Kampala and Helen  

Nyambura in Dar Es Salaam).

title: Kenya shilling recovers slightly on c.bank caution.
text:
NAIROBI, Aug 18 (Reuters) - The Kenya shilling bounced back marginally in early trade on Wednesday after the central bank warned it could intervene in the market to stabilise the local currency.  

The central bank's governor Andrew Mullei late on Tuesday blamed the local unit's recent fall to historic lows on speculation by commercial banks. He added that the bank would act to ensure the shilling is stable and purely determined by demand and supply.  

The shilling had raced to 80.60/80 to the dollar at Wednesday's open from 80.95/81.15 at Tuesday's close.  

But the local unit gave up some of those gains on the back of some light corporate dollar demand. At 0820 GMT it was quoted at 80.75/95 to the dollar, dealers said.  

"Nobody wants to take chances after the CBK (the Central Bank of Kenya) threatened to intervene," said Moses Kiboi, a senior dealer at Citibank.  

The shilling also received respite after some importers withdrew their orders for dollars when the shilling showed signs of firming, dealers said.  

The shilling has lost 3.8 percent of its value since the beginning of June when it was posted at a mean of 78.87 to the dollar compared to 81.13 on Tuesday.  

It has continued to set historic lows in recent weeks which the central bank said was not backed by fundamentals.  

Ramprasad Hasudi, the treasury manager at Commercial Bank of Africa, said he expected the shilling to strengthen further against the dollar but at a gradual pace because importer demand remained strong while export inflows were sluggish.  

"It will take a while because still the demand for dollars is there," he said. "We should not forget grain import is there."  

Currency dealers of late have blamed a number of factors on the shilling's fall, including a pending importer demand estimated at $50 million for 4 million 90-kg bags of maize.  

Political concerns, donor threats to pull aid from Kenya due to rising cases of corruption and high global oil prices have kept downward pressure on the shilling as well.  

A dealer at Imperial Bank said he expected the shilling to trade within a range of 80.60 and 81.10 in the short-term as long as importer demand continues to outweigh supply.

title: C.bank steadies Tanzania unit, Uganda,  Kenya  rise.
text:
NAIROBI, May 5 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention kept the Tanzanian shilling largely unchanged against the U.S. dollar in the week to Wednesday, while traders said the Ugandan and Kenyan currencies had strengthened.   

Leading banks in Tanzania's commercial capital Dar es Salaam posted the shilling at 1,115/1,118 per U.S. dollar, compared to 1,116/1,119 a week ago.   

"Last week corporates were looking to offload dollars to pay taxes, but the volume was not too big," said Shumbusho Rwezaura, a dealer at Stanbic Bank. "On the other hand, there was demand from all sectors. Whatever inflow came in was snapped up."   

Dealers said the central bank sold dollars on Friday at 1,115 shillings each to arrest a decline in the local currency, which had been posted at 1,119 per dollar at the close of trading on Thursday.   

"It appears central bank was not happy with the volatility caused by customers looking for dollars to make overseas payments," one dealer said, predicting that the shilling would stabilise between 1,113 and 1,120.   

The outlook was mixed, with Rwezaura saying he expected the shilling to break the psychological support level of 1,120 if the Bank of Tanzania did not make further dollars sales.   

"There is still demand in the office. Businessmen are a bit sceptical of the shilling breaking 1,120, so they are holding back demand. I see no reason why it should not break this level unless the central bank intervenes," he said.   

Uganda's shilling was stronger against the greenback over the week, trading at 1,890/1,900 shillings per dollar, compared to 1,906/12 shillings last Wednesday.   

Traders said the local unit had appreciated because the central Bank of Uganda (BOU) was selling dollars amid low corporate demand.   

"I don't think it is a massive intervention," said Lucas Ochieng, a trader at Barclays Bank. "The central bank gets project funds from donors which they have to disburse."   

Outlook was also mixed for the Ugandan unit, with dealers failing to agree on which direction the shilling was headed.   

"I think we will see the shilling appreciate because of a lack of demand for dollars and inflows (of dollars) from NGOs," said Joram Ssozi at Standard Chartered bank. "We have also seen some traders selling off their short positions."   

Another senior dealer in the capital Kampala said he expected to see the shilling retracing its steps as corporates, particularly from the construction and manufacturing sectors, come looking to buy dollars.   

The Kenya shilling also made gains against the dollar. At 1030 GMT banks it was trading at 78.25/45 shillings per dollar, up from 78.35/55 shillings last week.   

"Basically the shilling has been very stable this week," said Peter Mwaura, a senior dealer at Credit Agricole Indosuez bank. "There's not been much in the way of inflows (of dollars), and what there has been was matched by demand."   

Dealers said that in the absence of any market-moving news they saw the local currency rangebound in the week ahead.   

"I think the shilling will basically stay locked between 78.10 and 78.60," said Moses Kiboi at Kenya's Citibank.   

"We have tested the 78.50 support level for the shilling this week," said Kihara Maina, a dealer at Barclays Bank.   

"There may be one further test, but I think it might hold. On the other hand, I see resistance likely at 77.85."   

(Additional reporting by Helen Nyambura in Dar es Salaam).

title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW-Kenya cbank sees stable shg despite IMF delay.
text:
NAIROBI, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Kenya's central bank governor said on Thursday he expects the shilling to remain stable and competitive despite a decision by the International Monetary Fund to delay a meeting on lending.  

The shilling has fallen sharply, weakening to a one-month low after the IMF postponed by 16 days a meeting on whether to resume lending to the east African country.  

By Thursday, the shilling had fallen a total of 230 cents from 76.40/60 per dollar on Tuesday when Reuters broke news that the IMF had delayed the crucial meeting.  

In the first official reaction since the shilling's plunge, central bank governor Andrew Mullei told Reuters he was confident the IMF would re-open the credit lines, adding that the market had read too much into the postponement.  

"We expect the shilling to remain stable and competitive despite the postponement of IMF Board discussion on Kenya's request for IMF support," Mullei said in an interview.  

"It should be understood that postponement would not in any way imply rejection of the request."  

The governor did not give a forecast of what range he expects the shilling to trade. Last month he said the shilling was properly priced when it was posted at between 78.50/70 to the dollar.  

Kenyan and IMF officials said an Executive Board meeting in Washington scheduled for November 5 had been delayed until November 21. The Fund said it needed more time for more debt analysis on Kenya.  

Kenya is banking on winning a resumption of lending from the IMF after the lender froze its programme with Kenya in late 2000 over rampant government corruption.  

ANTI-GRAFT CRUSADE  

Kenyan President Mwai Kibaki has vowed to rebuild the country's battered economy and has made the fight against graft a key crusade of his administration in a bid to woo donors.  

Earlier this month Kibaki suspended half the country's top judges and set up special tribunals to investigate them, in a bold step to curb the vice. On Monday he said the day of reckoning for corrupt public officials was nigh.  

Mullei said the bank would continue with a policy of not intervening in the market to shore up the local currency.  

"Unlike the practice previously, CBK (Central Bank of Kenya) has not intervened in the market to influence the exchange rate in any way," he said. "With this policy, the shilling has held well against the major currencies, particularly the dollar."  

The governor admitted that the economy had not recovered "as fast as initially anticipated" due in part to the delay in donor support. But he added he expected a more rapid pick up in 2004 if donors resume lending.  

"Economic growth should start accelerating in the medium term," he said.  

Kenya's businesses have complained that wrangles in the ruling NARC coalition have dented business confidence and weighed down economic growth.  

The governor said the economy registered estimated growth of 1.4 percent in January-July 2003 compared with 0.7 percent for the same period of 2002.  

Mullei said the central bank would continue to pursue a low interest rate regime and strive to meet its target of an inflation of less than eight percent despite growing demand by government employees for salary increase.

The governor said the economy registered estimated growth of 1.4 percent in January-July 2003 compared to 0.7 percent for the same period of 2002.  

Mullei said the central bank would continue to pursue a low interest rate regime and strive to meet its target of an inflation of less than eight percent despite growing demand by government employees for salary increase.

title: UPDATE 1-Kenya cbank blames foreign banks for shilling fall.
text:
(Adds governor watching shilling, tells banks intervention possible, shilling falls further) 

 NAIROBI, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Kenya's central bank said on Wednesday the shilling's fall below a key psychological level was driven by speculation by foreign banks over election worries but he would not intervene at present to stop its fall. 

 Speaking to Reuters in an interview, Nahashon Nyagah added that although there was no need for intervention at the moment he was "watching" the shilling and might take action at an appropriate time in the future if banks failed to heed him. 

 "Players in the foreign exchange market are playing into the hands of foreign banks," Nyagah said. 

 "I have identified the problem is foreign banks from South Africa, Middle East, London and New York. It is not because of fundamental reasons. It is speculative." 

 Nyagah blamed foreign banks for undermining the rate of the shilling based on the perception that Kenya's political future was uncertain due to elections slated for December 27. 

 Dealers reacted to his remarks by pushing the shilling shilling below a nine-year low of 80.10/20 to the dollar hit on Tuesday when the currency sank under the key psychological mark of 80 for the first time in almost a decade. 

 Dealers said Tuesday's fall was driven by unusually high dollar demand and a dearth of export earnings. At the close on Wednesday it stood at 80.05/25 after briefly touching 80.50/55. 

 In recent months the local unit has stood at about 79.50/55. 

 Kenya holds crucial general elections on December 27 when veteran President Daniel arap Moi is due to step down after 24 years in power, and his ruling party is facing is toughest battle yet against a united opposition. 

 "Electioneering is the excuse," he said. "What uncertainties are there? There is none. Kenya has held elections every five years since independence, and if it is the transition, President Moi has already said he will retire, so there is no uncertainty." 

 Nyagah said he would not use the around $1 billion or 3.4 months cover in foreign exchange reserves to influence the rate. 

 "I will not intervene," Nyagah said, repeating the phrase throughout the interview. 

 He said to intervene given present market sentiment would only fuel the unit's slide, and instead urged banks to exercise restraint and not rush to trade at present rates. 

 But the governor offered to sell dollars to individual banks that run into dollar shortfalls. 

 "There is no need for intervention at the moment, but I am watching," he said. "I will offer to sell to them (Kenyan banks) dollars at an agreed exchange rate to cover any liquidity shortfall that they have." 

 He said he could meet up to $50 million a day if need be to cover any gaps in their books. 

 He also said that there might come a time when he would contemplate intervention. "At an appropriate time, if the banks do not hear my appeal, I will come in," Nyagah said. 

 DEALERS PREDICT FURTHER FALL 

 Some dealers said the decision not to intervene immediately to stem the shilling's drop would fuel further speculative buying by foreign banks. 

 "Not intervening gives the speculators the okay to raid the market," said one dealer who declined to be named. 

 "I'm just surprised that he won't intervene. I think we shall see the shilling weaken to 81 by Thursday." 

 Dealers said they had expected the governor to sell dollars into the market to stem the currency's plunge as promised earlier. 

 In late October, the CBK governor told Reuters that the bank would intervene to keep the currency exchange rate below the psychological level of 80 shillings. 

 "Too little too late on verbal intervention, we have already breached the psychological level of 80," said James Mutuku a senior dealer at Kenya Commercial Bank. 

 "Verbal intervention is hot air, and players now know the central bank will never intervene actively. The shilling is likely to go into a tailspin." 

 Some dealers said it was a positive statement for free markets. 

 "It's a positive statement as it lets the market to determine its own level," Fred Michuki, head of trading at Standard Chartered said. 

 "I think it will turn at the appropriate time, but for now dollar demand will rise because you cannot wish away the political jitters that investors have."

title: INTERVIEW-Kenya cenbank sees stable shilling ahead of poll.
text:
DAR ES SALAAM, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Kenya's central bank chief said on Friday the shilling would end the year below a key psychological level despite pressure from impending elections. 

 Nahashon Nyagah told Reuters in Tanzania's capital Dar Es Salaam that the country's currency would range-trade from 78 to 79 shillings per dollar, just under the key psychological level of 80 shillings despite steady weakening since August. 

 "I don't think it will hit the 80 (shillings) mark against the dollar," Nyagah said. 

 Kenya is expected to hold general elections in December when veteran President Daniel arap Moi is due to step down after 24 years at the helm and the local unit has weakened as the market reacts to the uncertainty of change. 

 But Nyagah said there were no economic fundamentals to indicate the shilling should weaken further and said the central bank would intervene to halt any swings in the exchange rate that are not supported by fundamentals. 

 "In the past one and a half years we have not had to intervene in a single day, we do not want to," Nyagah said. 

Kenya's central bank does not usually reveal when it intervenes in the market but has repeatedly warned banks it could use its relatively strong $1.1 billion of foreign exchange reserves to influence the rate. 

 Nyagah also moved to reassure investors that the central bank is independent of the government and would not suffer any attempts to fiddle with monetary policy for electoral reasons. 

 He said legislation barred the central bank from printing money to fund the forthcoming elections, as happened in the run-up to the 1992 elections when Moi's government printed money to finance the ruling party's campaign, creating a deep post-election economic slump. 

 "It is not a request I have received from the government, it will not happen and it will never happen as long as I am governor," Nyagah said. 

 He said lack of international donor support was partly to blame for Kenya's sputtering economy, which grew at a modest 1.2 percent in 2001 compared with 5.6 percent in Tanzania. But he added he expected lending to Kenya to resume early next year when a new parliament is constituted. 

 Officials hope the new parliament will conclude the passage of anti-corruption bills demanded by the International Monetary Fund, whose blessing is a key criteria for many donors. 

 The Corruption Control Bill 2002, which sets up an independent anti-corruption body and the Public Officers' Ethics Bill which demands that all senior public servants including the president declare their wealth, have been pending in parliament despite passing several crucial stages of debate. 

 "The bills are ready to go to parliament, and that is all we have left and once parliament is back I see that we'll be able to get back on the IMF programme so I see the economy getting much better," Nyagah said. 

Currency analysts were not in total agreement with Nyagah. 

 Some say the shilling will breach 80 shillings by the end of the year. But most agree it will not weaken much further. 

 Leading commercial banks posted the shilling at a mean rate of 79.55/65 to the dollar at 0800 GMT from 79.25/50 at Thursday's close. 

 Dealers said the market was edgy and attributed the shilling's falls to interbank speculation as banks move to stock up on dollars ahead of the weekend. 

 "The shilling is expected to remain under pressure as dealers square positions ahead of the weekend," Citibank said in a Friday market report.

title: Tanzania shilling little changed vs dollar.
text:
NAIROBI, Oct 9 (Reuters) - The Tanzania shilling was little changed against the dollar on Wednesday compared with a week ago but found support from export earnings, dealers said. The Kenyan shilling eased a touch versus the greenback over the past seven days amid lower tea exports. 

 At 0830 GMT leading commercial banks posted the local unit at 976/977 shillings to the dollar slightly firmer from last Wednesday's close of 977/978. 

 They said Tanzanian shilling gains were expected to continue on export earnings, while the Kenyan shilling struggled back from a three-month low on Monday. 

 "The (Tanzanian) shilling has appreciated slightly because it is the peak of the cashew nut and coffee crop season," said Alex Ngusaru at Tanzania's Citibank, adding that there had not been much corporate demand for dollars. 

 Dealers said the Tanzanian shilling has also been pressured this week by the Bank of Tanzania, which bought dollars in the market on Monday and Tuesday for the second week running to restrain the shilling's rise. 

 "They intervened to release pressure on the shilling to appreciate," said Ngusaru. 

 Dealers said they expected the Tanzanian shilling to remain buoyant while central bank intervention continues. 

 The Kenya shilling was down 10 Kenyan cents overall in the week at 79.10/20 shillings to the greenback from last Wednesday's close of 79.00/10 shillings, but had fought back from low of 79.40/50 on Monday. 

 Dealers said dwindling tea export receipts and a need for dollars by the Kenya Tea Development Agency (KTDA) to make foreign payments hit the shilling. 

 Tea is Kenya's leading foreign exchange earner. 

 "The (Kenyan) shilling edged lower to...79.40/50 shillings as tea inflows continue to dwindle, owing to poor weather conditions in August and September," a dealer at Barclays Bank of Kenya said. 

 Dealers said they expected the Kenya shilling to strengthen in the coming week as corporates shy away from dollar buying at present rates and as KTDA's dollar receipts improve. 

 "The shilling is bound to strengthen as inflows come in and as people sitting on dollars sell them to take advantage of the high rates," said the dealer at Barclays bank. 

 "Corporates will then come in to buy dollars at better prices." 

 Traders predicted Kenya's shilling would remain rangebound between 79.10/25 in the coming week. 

 Banks in Uganda were closed on Wednesday as the country is celebrating its independence from British colonial rule.

title: UPDATE 1- Kenya  shilling gains on  intervention  talk.
text:
NAIROBI, June 14 (Reuters) - The Kenya shilling bounced from near 18-month lows on Friday, gaining up to 70 cents against the dollar as traders reacted to a report that the central bank said it had the resources to support the local unit. 

 The shilling hit a peak of 78.60/70 to the dollar in early trade compared to 79.30/40 at Thursday's close. At 1220 GMT the shilling eased slightly to 78.80/90 to the dollar. 

 The local unit had depreciated sharply as importers bought dollars as a precaution ahead of the budget. 

 The central bank governor Nahashon Nyaga was quoted by the East African Standard daily as saying he had adequate resources to intervene in the market and correct the shilling's depreciation. 

 There was no immediate comment from Nyagah. 

 Anthony Wachira of Kenya Commercial Bank's treasury department said the shilling had gained on the report. 

 "To a large extent the shilling's gain was prompted by the central bank's threat of intervention," said Wachira. 

 "There is a likelihood it will strengthen even further because the clear signal from central bank is that the shilling should be stronger at levels of about 78.30/40." 

 Kenya's foreign exchange reserves have risen steadily to $1.077 billion by March 2002 or 3.4 months of import cover. 

 But other dealers attributed the gains to a correction after the budget announcement on Thursday by Finance Minister Chris Obure for 2002/03 came in at the market's expectations. 

 Traders said a rise in Kenya's budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2001/02 (July-June) from a 1.8 percent deficit the previous year was slightly better than market expectations. 

 "People overspeculated on the budget - since it was going up on hot air it had to go down on hot air," said Maina Kihara at Barclays Bank. 

 The shilling touched 79.45/50 early in Thursday's session, its lowest level for 18 months, as fears over the size of the gap in government finances weighed. The local unit last hit 79.50 to the dollar on December 7, 2000. 

 "I think the market was driving up the dollar against the shilling on the premise that there would be a huge budget deficit that would therefore impact on how the shilling should behave," Kihara said. 

 "But yesterday there was really nothing new. Everyone knew there was going to be a budget deficit." 

 The widened budget deficit reflected increasing spending ahead of elections due this year and a funding gap left by the suspension of donor lending in 2000 over corruption concerns. 

 Traders said the size of the deficit was roughly in line with expectations. 

 "The only thing I can put it down to is that this is a speculator's market," said Fred Michuki at Standard Chartered Bank, adding that all the activity in Friday's busy market was down to interbank players. 

 "There has been a lot of talk pre-budget, as in the last few years, and the shilling tends to weaken before a budget and strengthen after it. There are no fundamentals."

title: Energy sector keeps Kenya shilling under pressure.
text:
NAIROBI, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling shed 15 cents to 78.75/95 against the dollar in early Wednesday trade, pressured by energy sector demand, but traders were wary of central bank intervention above the 79.0 level. 

 The unit opened at the same level on Tuesday, but ended higher at 78.60/80 after inflows from the tea sector. 

 Traders said those inflows and some from aid organisations and the horticulture sector were still coming in and in sufficient amounts to steady the shilling. 

 "There is a quite a bit of activity from the oil and energy (electricity) sectors," said Noah Meely at ABN Amro. 

 Dealers say traditional month-end demand for dollars has been heightened by the rising demand of the oil sector due to higher crude oil prices and greater oil use in power generation because of a drought. 

 But they said caution reigned in the market that the Central Bank of Kenya could intervene if the shilling breached the 79.0 to the dollar level. 

 "Resistance is there because of fear of central bank intervention," said another dealer who declined to be named. 

 The shilling has been vulnerable this year due to falling tea output and lower coffee prices, two of Kenya's main foreign exchange earners. 

 But hard currency demand from the corporate sector has also been curtailed by the impact of Kenya's worst drought in four decades which has slowed economic growth.

title: Kenya  shilling decline braked by  intervention  fear.
text:
NAIROBI, June 30 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling held steady against the dollar in quiet trade on Friday and traders said players were cautious, fearing central bank intervention. 

 The shilling fell through 78.0 against the greenback on Thursday, a key support level. 

 At 0945 GMT it was posted at 77.90/78.10 unchanged from Thursday's close. 

 "People think a fall towards 78.50 is not sustainable because the central bank might intervene," said one dealer. 

 "It is a question of once bitten twice shy," he added, recalling last month when the Central Bank of Kenya sold dollars after the shilling touched the 78 level. 

 A surge in demand for dollars as corporates rushed to meet end of month commitments lowered the shilling on Thursday. 

 But other dealers said the local currency was supported by sentiment that key donors could restart funding to Kenya soon. 

 They said the market was likely to remain dull during the rest of the session with most people just squaring positions ahead of the weekend. 

 The central bank posted the shilling at a mean commercial rate of 77.95 to the dollar.

title: Kenya shilling seen on defensive ahead of budget.
text:
NAIROBI, May 31 (Reuters) - The Kenyan shilling will remain on the defensive ahead of the 1999/2000 state budget on June 10, undermined by higher importer demand and shortfalls in agriculture exports, currency analysts said on Monday. 

 They said they saw the shilling in the 69 to 71 range against the dollar, with any breach of 72 expected to trigger central bank intervention in the market. 

 The shilling opened lower again on Monday with commercial banks quoting it at 70.80/71.05 against the dollar. 

 "The shilling remains vulnerable to reduced dollar sales by exporters, believed to be withholding funds from the market in the hope of benefiting from further shilling softness," said Razia Khan, of the Standard Chartered Bank in London. 

 "The recent experience of rapid weakening will likely see sustained importer demand for forward cover, reinforcing the shilling's downward bias," added Khan, a treasury economist. 

 Kenya's financial markets and foreign donors hope the government will present a budget that includes concrete measures to cut government spending, rebuild the crumbling infrastructure and improve its supervision of commercial banks. 

 A good budget would likely boost the shilling even though the export sector remains weak. 

 Dealers said the shilling has been hurt by developments in the tea and coffee sectors - Kenya's main commodity exports. 

 They said low world coffee prices and a dispute on marketing rules among smallholder coffee societies were likely to offset the advantages of increased production. 

 Smallholders produce about half Kenya's total coffee crop. 

 The outlook for tea, the top hard-currency earner, was also gloomy. Despite a forecast recovery from below-average rains earlier this year, Kenya could face the loss of an important export market. 

 Retaliatory measures in response to tariffs imposed on Pakistani rice by Kenya have led to lobbying by the Pakistani Chamber of Commerce to impose similar tariffs on Kenyan tea. 

 The Pakistani decision has not been finalised and could contravene World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules. But the last two months have witnessed a fall in Pakistani purchases at Kenyan tea auctions, depressing competition and keeping prices low. 

 Markets are also awaiting the resumption of International Monetary Fund (IMF) lending to Kenya, on which hopes have long been placed to boost investor confidence and domestic growth. 

 The IMF board of directors met Kenyan Treasury officials this month in Washington but failed to set a date for the resumption of talks on the stalled three-year $205 million loan under its Enhanced Structural Adjustment facility (ESAF). 

 "The shilling will continue its downward trajectory in the absence of positive news from that front," said a senior dealer at a bank in Nairobi. "That news should be available in July." 

 Hints by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) that intervention would be forthcoming if the shilling reached an unacceptable level, thought to be around 70 versus the dollar, have helped to shore up support for the currency in the past, analysts said. 

 The central bank says it will only smooth out fluctuations in the exchange rate not caused by economic fundamentals, rather than attempt to set a direction for the currency. 

 The central bank has blamed shilling losses mainly on a rapid decline in interest rates. The yield on the benchmark 91-day treasury bills now stands at below 10 percent from a peak of 27 percent in April last year. 

 CBK Chief Dealer Charles Musau told reporters this month that low interest rates meant offshore dollars were now chasing markets offering better yields - and that put constant pressure on the shilling.

title: Kenya shilling stable against dollar.
text:
NAIROBI, May 4 (Reuters) - The Kenya shilling was steady against the dollar in thin trade on Tuesday as the local unit found support at the 67 level. 

 At 0930 GMT five leading banks posted the shilling at 67.65/75 against the dollar, slightly firmer from Monday's close of 67.80/95. 

 The shilling found support at 67 after the easing of a surge last week in demand for dollars, dealers said. Profit-taking had also lent support to the shilling, they said. 

 "We have seen exporters locking foward deals (at the same rate)," one dealer said. 

 The Kenya shilling fell to an average of 67.44 to the dollar in the week to Tuesday from 65.77 in the same period the previous week, the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) said. 

 The bank said it would not intervene in the market to prop up the shilling. 

 But it could enter the market to purchase foreign exchange for three reasons - to cater for government and its maturing obligations, to increase bank reserves and to smooth over wide fluctuations in the shilling arising from non-economic fundamentals, it said. 

 "We still maintain our policy of leaving the shilling exchange rate to be determined by market forces of supply and demand," CBK's chief economist Maurice Kanga said in a statement. 

 Last week, dollar purchases to meet foreigners' portfolio investment leaving the market after sharp declines in treasury bills yield sent the shilling 2.5 percent lower against the dollar. 

 The central bank hinted it would come into the market if the shilling looked like falling to the 70 level, comments that dealers said had helped shore up the local unit. 

 The central bank posted a shilling mean indicative rate of 67.55 to the dollar from 67.61 at Monday's open. 

 Against the pound and euro, the bank quoted a shilling mean commercial rate of 108.96 and 71.56 respectively from 108.86 and 71.56 on Monday. ((Nairobi newsroom, +254 2 330261/2 fax +254 2 338860, nairobi.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS -  Kenya  cen.bank  intervenes  after shilling fall.
text:
NAIROBI, Dec 14 (Reuters) - The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) intervened in the foreign exchange market on Monday, selling dollars after a speculative attack forced a sharp fall in the shilling. 

 "The central bank intervened in the market, selling some dollars. But the action came late and did not have the desired effect," said a senior dealer at a leading international bank. 

 There was no immediate word from CBK on the intervention. Dealers did not say at what rate the central bank sold dollars but added that Kenyan currency strengthened by up to a shilling against the dollar afterwards. 

 The shilling fell to its lowest level of the day at 64.00/65.50 against the dollar at 3:00 p.m. (1200 GMT), shortly before the intervention, before settling at 63.50/64.50. 

 At 0900 GMT, four leading banks had posted the shilling at 62.80/63.35 against the dollar while two other banks were quoting 62.70/63.10 from 62.40/62.90 on Friday. 

 "There was a speculative attack by some South African banks, they hit the market on Friday and this morning and returned later to take their profits," one treasurer told Reuters. 

 Another dealer said that the market remained nervous and there was a possibility of further central bank intervention early on Tuesday to stem any further shilling declines. 

 "There are just a few South Africans playing around the market and influencing the frenetic movement of the last few hours," the dealer said. 

 Dealers said the huge spreads - between a shilling and 1.50 shillings - reflected the nervous state of the market. They added that it was too early to say what direction the shilling would take due to uncertainty on further CBK intervention plans. 

 Earlier, dealers said a decline in treasury bill yields had forced a complimentary decline in the shilling rate. 

 "The steady decline in interest rates on treasury bills is putting pressure on the local unit," Chris Rengo, chief dealer at Standard Chartered Bank, told Reuters. 

 The average yield on Kenya's benchmark 91-day treasury bill fell to 12.959 percent last Thursday from 14.349 percent the previous week. The 12-week moving average of the 91-day T-bill yield fell to 18.330 percent, from 19.113 percent last week. 

 Dealers said unrelenting corporate demand supported by some interest for dollars from offshore banks had convinced exporters to hold on to their dollars, hoping to offload when the greenback is at its peak. 

 They said sentiment was for a weaker shilling. 

 Another dealer said he had noted demand for dollars from the oil sector with players looking to buy crude oil at the current very low prices. 

 The central bank posted a shilling opening mean indicative rate of 62.3461 to the dollar from 61.6683 on Friday. 

 ((Nairobi newsroom, +254 2 330261/2 fax +254 2 338860, nairobi.newsroom@reuters.com)).
