title: AFRICA  FX  WEEKAHEAD-Kenya, Uganda shillings stay under pressure
text:
NAIROBI, July 7 (Reuters) - Kenya's and Uganda's shillings are likely to come under pressure against the dollar next week, while Tanzania's steadily weakening currency may take brief respite after unusually stiff central bank intervention.

KENYA

Kenya's shilling <KES=> is seen weaker against the dollar next week, pressured by expected dollar demand from the energy sector and maize importers, traders said.

Kenya is predicting increased maize importation after the government removed duties in June to address shortages and rising prices of the staple. [ID:nLDE75K0FF]

At 0822 GMT, the shilling was posted at 89.75/89.85 against the dollar, weaker than last Thursday's close of 89.35/55.

"At the moment energy sector and also maize sector dollar demand might come in, pushing the currency weaker. We might see a weaker shilling in the coming week," said Bhavin Chandaria, a trader at Imperial Bank.

Central Bank Governor Njuguna Ndung'u said on Thursday that poor reading of information by market participants was to blame for fresh shilling weakness against the dollar. [ID:nLDE7660P8]

Traders said they expected the shilling to trade in the 89.80-91.00 range.

The shilling has gained since the central bank raised its overnight lending rate to 8.0 percent, lifting it off a record low of 91.90 against the dollar on June 22. [ID:nLDE75S0QW]

"The shilling seems to be in dire straits again and is likely to be dragged lower if other dollar buyers join the fray," Commercial Bank of Africa said in a note.

UGANDA

The Uganda shilling will stay under pressure against the dollar next week, despite the introduction of a new benchmark lending rate, traders in the capital, Kampala, said.

The Bank of Uganda launched the inaugural benchmark interest rate of 13 percent and a 5 percent core inflation target on Wednesday in a bid to tame price pressures that pushed inflation to a 17-year high in May.

But with dollar inflows expected to remain tight and demand from the oil sector high, traders do not see it having an immediate impact on what the central bank says is an undervalued currency.

The shilling sold for 2,600/2,620 to the dollar towards the end of trade on Thursday.

"Unless the fundamentals change I see it holding at these levels," Lucas Ochieng, treasurer at Orient Bank Uganda, said. "Liquidity is still the issue, so even given the introduction of the CBR, we will still see the status quo."

Some analysts had said it might take the Ugandan shilling time to respond, but that the tight monetary policy stance meant the currency should continue its climb from June's all-time lows against the dollar.

"There will be more pressure next week," Faisal Bukenya, head of market making at Barclays Uganda, said. "We're not seeing the inflows."

Traders, though, did expect a pick-up in interest for short-term paper from offshore investors.

The shilling slipped to a record low of 2,710 against the dollar last week on strong dollar demand from the oil sector, speculative trading and panic buying before the central bank stepped in and sold dollars.

TANZANIA

Tanzania's shilling <TZS=> is expected to hold steady after firming slightly against the dollar on Wednesday after the central bank moved to calm the market.

Commercial banks quoted it at 1,600/1,605 to the dollar at Wednesday's close, after earlier trading at an all-time low of 1,625.

Markets are closed in Tanzania on Thursday for a public holiday.

"The central bank governor met bankers this week and told them that he would like to see the shilling trading below 1,600 in the interbank market," United Bank of Africa Tanzania dealer Bernard Charo said, referring to one of the regular meetings held with the central bank.

On Wednesday, the central bank traded $17.85 million on its interbank market, more than double its daily average amount for the year, traders said.

But traders said they did not expect the central bank to sustain higher dollar sales after the government said it did not want to deplete foreign exchange reserves. [ID:nLDE75K207]

"Some corporate customers are standing aside, waiting for the shilling to continue to depreciate before they come in with their demand for dollars," said Johnvian Nyamsisa, a trader at Commercial Bank of Africa Tanzania.

"The shilling might go to 1,590-1,600 levels next week if the current demand slowdown continues."

In the week to Wednesday, the Bank of Tanzania traded $45.55 million on the Interbank FX Market, according to its website.

ZAMBIA

The kwacha <ZMK=> is expected to firm as foreign investors convert dollars in order to pay local taxes.

Commercial banks quoted the currency of Africa's leading copper producer at 4,820, marginally up from 4,830 to the dollar a week ago.

"The local currency is likely to post some gains against the dollar with the anticipated increase in dollar supply from corporates who will be converting foreign currency for kwacha in order meet statutory obligations," Cavmont bank treasurer Mudenda Syamujaye said.

The kwacha has traded between 4,800 and 4,600 for most of this year. During 2010 it met firm resistance at 4,600. On the few occasions it breached that level it went on to test, but failed to breach, 4,550.

GHANA

The cedi <GHS=> is seen holding firm against the dollar ahead of the issue of a 5-year bond open to foreigners on July 28, traders said.

The unit is likely to close the week at 1.5160 versus the greenback and will remain steady at that level, said Jacob Brobbey of Barclays Ghana.

"We see rates tamed in the $1.5120-$1.5160 band in the coming weeks," he said.

Ghana's central bank has announced plans to issue a 300 million cedi bond on July 28, the first 5-year note since December 2007.

On Wednesday, the bank's Monetary Policy Committee announced a 50 basis point cut on its benchmark rate to 12.5 percent, which analysts said boosted the resilience of the cedi.

Biggles Amponsah of Access Bank Ghana projected a balanced dollar flows.

"I will also expect traders to start shorting the dollar in smaller volumes ahead of the bond issue. This should be sufficient reason to hold the local currency against the dollar amidst rising demand," he said.

NIGERIA

The naira <NGN=D1> is seen losing ground as traders miss out on dollars expected to be sold by state-oil firm NNPC, which instead went to the central bank.

The state-owned energy company usually sells dollars to some lenders on a monthly basis and transfers the naira proceeds to its account with the central bank. NNPC dollar sales usually form the bulk of supplies to the interbank market.

The local currency was trading at 153.32 to the dollar on the interbank on Thursday compared with 152.60 at Wednesday's close as traders contended with lower-than-expected month-end dollar inflows.

"With the NNPC funds no longer available for trading at the interbank market, the naira will definitely depreciate further in the coming days," one currency trader said.

Dealers said the naira should trade within a 153-153.90 band.

"We are hoping that some foreign investors bring in dollars next week to help provide some liquidity in the market in view of the present reality and cushion the impact of the absence of NNPC dollars in the market," another dealer said.

The naira appreciated to its strongest level in six months last week after the central bank initiated measures aimed at boosting dollar supply, reducing pressure on the local currency.

The central bank this month lifted a rule that foreign investors hold government debt for at least one year, a move which is expected to attract new offshore flows, boosting dollar supply and increasing demand for the naira.

The central bank also imposed a maximum weekly limit of $250,000 in dollar sales by banks to foreign exchange bureaux, a move which traders said was to check money laundering and capital flight, contributing to naira support.

(Reporting by Kevin Mwanza, Fumbuka Ng'wanakilala, Barry Malone, Chris Mfula, Oludare Mayowa and Kwasi Kpodo, editing by Ed Cropley)

title: UPDATE 1-Kenya tourism arrivals up 16 pct in Jan-April
text:
* Kenya shilling weakness could boost sector - minister

* Tourism up after 2008 violence, global financial crisis

NAIROBI, June 28 (Reuters) - The number of tourists visiting Kenya in the first four months of 2011 rose by 16 percent from a year earlier, and a weaker local currency could boost the number of visitors in the short term, the tourism minister said on Tuesday.

Tourist arrivals in east Africa's biggest economy rose to 390,148 from 336,179 in the same period a year earlier.

Tourism generated 74 billion shillings ($817.6 million) in 2010 for east Africa's biggest economy, making it one of the country's leading sources of foreign exchange.

The sector has recovered after it was hit in 2008 by post-election violence and the lingering effects of the global financial crisis, which hurt arrivals in 2009.

"These figures shows positive growth," Tourism Minister Najib Balala told reporters.

Balala said the weakening of the shilling could benefit the sector, but warned that the wider implications of a weaker shilling on the economy could increase the cost of living.

"When the shilling is too weak ... it can be good for one sector but not necessarily for the entire economy and the people of Kenya, so we need to find a balance," he said.

"Definitely there will be an increase of interest (from tourists) but I don't believe that this is the main reason (for the growth in tourist arrivals). The weakening of the shilling is temporary," he said.

Balala said he backed the central bank's policy of not intervening to prop up the shilling against the dollar, but noted that prices of food imports were likely to rise.

The shilling hit a new low against the dollar of 91.90 last Wednesday, but the central bank has resisted intervening in the foreign exchange market by selling hard currency to stem the shilling's slide.

The bank has said Kenya had adequate foreign exchange reserves but would only intervene to stabilise currency volatility, not to influence the level or direction of the shilling.

title: UPDATE 2-Kenyan c.bank says has acted on  fx  speculation
text:
* Says has taken action to stop arbitrage

* Says further tightening being considered

(Adds more quotes, analyst)

By Duncan Miriri

NAIROBI, June 23 (Reuters) - Kenya's central bank has taken unspecified action against some commercial banks to curb speculative positions versus the currency of east Africa's largest economy, its governor said on Thursday.

The shilling hit a new low against the dollar of 91.90 on Wednesday but recovered on Thursday to end at 90.1 after a report the central bank would take steps to stem the trades.

"We have taken action on them and we cannot talk about what action we have taken because it's regulatory. We have taken proper action on them, appropriate to the law, and we'll continuously do that," Governor Njuguna Ndung'u told a news conference. "We are not afraid to do that again."

The market had closed before he made these comments.

Inflation in Kenya has surged into double-digits this year reaching 12.95 percent in May. Short-dated Treasury bond yields have jumped into double-digits and the shilling has lost more than 10 percent since 2010.

The central bank measures follow an audit of banks' trading positions. Ndung'u said that during the week of June 9, five banks exported $260 million while borrowing from the central bank's window by strong banks went up -- pointing to arbitrage.

"These positions do not seem to reflect trading fundamentals. This type of exposure will put pressure on the exchange rate ... We will restrict them from any arbitrage using the domestic currency," he said. "We cannot ratify arbitrage."

Under the law establishing the central bank, the regulator can direct the management of a commercial bank to provide a viable explanation for any adverse effects in the market, and even speculative behaviour, the governor has said.

He has said that if such speculative behaviour were not halted, section 32 A of the Banking Act gave the central bank the power to act. The section allows the regulator to apply sanctions up to disqualification against people managing or controlling financial institutions.

TIGHTER POLICY?

"The arbitrage opportunity -- that has allowed banks with healthy liquidity positions to borrow cheaply at the overnight window of the CBK, and reinvest proceeds in higher yielding short-term T-bills, or fund other trades -- has been identified," said Razia Khan, head of Africa research at Standard Chartered Bank in London.

"Although it is unclear just yet how the authorities will deal with this, some tightening of liquidity should be anticipated," she said.

The central bank has resisted intervening in the foreign exchange market by selling hard currency to stem the shilling's slide. Ndung'u said Kenya had adequate foreign exchange reserves but could only intervene to stabilise currency volatility, rather than the level or direction of the shilling.

He said the bank might in future consider further tightening of monetary policy if inflation was not tame.

"But we are seeing signs ... that even though inflation will not come down drastically, the signs are inflation will come down and we are waiting on inflationary expectations."

The central bank cut its benchmark lending rate by 25 basis points in January but reversed the move in March and raised rates by another 25 basis points in May to 6.25 percent.

"With the regulator now taking firmer action against continued shilling depreciation -- albeit still within the confines of allowing markets to determine the FX rate -- a lower peak in inflation appears more likely," said Khan.

"Actual shilling appreciation would, however, be needed to meaningfully improve the near term inflation outlook," she said.

(Additional reporting by Kevin Mwanza and Richard Lough; editing by David Clarke and Stephen Nisbet

title: UPDATE 1-C.bank: Kenya  shilling  intervention  would worsen matters
text:
* Says euro zone fears boosting dollar

 * Sees no direct remedy to shilling's fall

 * Rejects claims that CBK does not care about rate

(Adds governor's quotes, details)

 By Duncan Miriri

 NAIROBI, June 20 (Reuters) - Intervening in the market at this stage to prop up Kenya's shilling <KES=> would make things worse for the currency as some of its problems stem from concerns about the euro zone, the central bank governor said.

 The shilling was quoted by commercial banks at 90.10/30 against the dollar at 0903 GMT, following his remarks, weaker than Friday's closing level of 89.70/80.

 The Kenyan currency has lost more than 10 percent against the dollar this year on the back of high inflation, prompting concerns the weakening could give rise to a spiral in inflation through higher import costs.

 It fell to record lows against the greenback last week, touching 90.85 on Thursday.

 Kenya's central bank has sought to boost its foreign reserves in recent months by buying hard currency in the foreign exchange market, while also tightening shilling liquidity via repurchase agreements.

Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) governor Njuguna Ndung'u said the debt and deficit crisis in the euro zone had worked to the dollar's advantage, with its appeal as a reserve currency benefiting from concerns about the euro.

 "This is bidding its price up and weakening the shilling and other currencies. So there is no direct remedy until we wait for the euro fears to subside, intervention will worsen the situation at this stage," he said in a statement to Reuters.

 "This has put pressure on the shilling to depreciate on one hand and creates inflationary pressure on the other hand."

 The pressure on domestic prices is coming from pass-through effects, especially from fuel and commodity prices, which were exacerbated by uncertainties in the market and pressure from a weaker shilling, he said.

 Year-on-year inflation rose to 12.95 percent in May from 12.05 percent in the previous month. [ID:nLDE74U07O]

 Ndung'u rejected claims by some analysts and traders that the central bank does not care about the currency movements and that if it did, it would intervene. [ID:nLDE7580LQ]

 "The CBK is monitoring the situation very closely from the domestic market to international developments," he said.

 The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee adopted a tightening stance in March, reversing a 25 basis point cut made in January. It then raised its rate by a further quarter point last month to 6.25 percent, and increased the amount of cash that banks are required to hold. [ID:nLDE74U1TR] 

 It expects the tightening policy to fight inflation and stabilise the exchange rate, Ndung'u said last week.

title: UPDATE 3-Kenya shilling plunges to new record low vs dollar
text:
* Shilling hits 91 after central bank says no intervention

* Oil sector dollar demand seen weighing on the shilling

* Stocks flat on weak economic outlook

(Recast with markets close, stocks, bonds)

By Kevin Mwanza

NAIROBI, June 20 (Reuters) - The Kenyan shilling <KES=> tumbled to a record low of 91.00 against the dollar on Monday after the central bank said it would not intervene to prop up the shilling, traders said.

Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) Governor Njuguna Ndung'u said intervening in the market at this stage to prop up the shilling would make things worse for the currency as some of its problems stem from concerns about the euro zone. [ID:nLDE75J0O6]

At close of trade at 1300 GMT, the shilling was quoted at the session low of 91.0, a 1.4 percent depreciation from Friday's close of 89.7.

"I think the move started on the back of central bank comments that made the market panic some more," said a senior trader at one commercial bank who did not want to be named.

Ndung'u was reacting to analyst comments that the bank needed to do more than just increase interest rates to counter a vicious inflation shock that has driven an 11.6 percent slide in the shilling this year. [ID:nLDE7580LQ]

The central bank had also planned to mop up 0.5 billion shillings ($5.6 million) through repurchase agreements, but rejected all the bids for the third straight session. <CBK04>

The bank's repurchase agreements, or repos, basically take shillings out of the market to tighten liquidity.

Traders said earlier that interbank trading limits were tight following aggressive trading last week that saw the shilling touch a string of all-time lows.

They said the shilling could face further pressure this week as end-month corporate demand for dollars, especially form the oil sector, came in to the market.

"There is no liquidity in the market. It dried on the governor's comments. In a sane environment, the resistance would be 92. But now the sky is the limit," said Chris Muiga, senior trader at Kenya Commercial Bank.

"Corporate end-month demand from the oil sector may keep the shilling under pressure this week," said Steve Lagat, a trader at CFC Stanbic Bank.

On the Nairobi Stock Exchange, the benchmark NSE-20 Share Index <.NSE20> was barely changed, edging slightly up by 0.03 percent to 3,986.05 points.

Analysts said the weaker economic outlook due to the rising inflation rate and the volatile shilling was affecting market activities on the bourse.

"The market is very bearish and its being affected by the performance of the shilling and a high inflation rate," said Renaldo D'souza of Genghis Capital.

"Rising interest rates in the fixed income market has also curbed new investment from the equities market."

Yields on Treasury bills have been on the rise for the last few weeks, but started easing lasting week after the central bank said the cost of government debt had become too expensive. [ID:nLDE75F1MB]

Shares in Williamson Tea rose 3.81 percent to 218 shillings after it announced a 9 percent rise in full-year pretax profits, boosted by an increase in property valuations. [ID:nLDE75J05R]

Barclays Bank of Kenya shares rose 2.07 percent to 17.25 shillings a share on foreign investors buys, traders said.

Corporate and Treasury bonds valued at 2.82 billion shillings ($31.4 million) were traded on the stock exchange, down from 4.805 billion shillings on Friday.

NAIROBI, May 19 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling could hit new lows against the dollar next week while its Ugandan peer will probably have to rely on central bank intervention to stay on an even keel.

KENYA

Kenya's shilling <KES=>, which hit all-time lows on Wednesday and Thursday, is expected to keep weakening if the central bank continues to buy foreign currency and importers step up dollar buying as usual towards the end of the month.

The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) has bought 28 million euros and mopped up 6 billion shillings, which it said on Thursday was meant to build reserves and cover for external payments amounting to $9.1 million. [ID:nLDE74I0F1]

At 1226 GMT, commercial banks quoted the shilling at 86.20/30 against the dollar, after it earlier hit an all-time low of 87.15 sparked by central bank purchases of euros.

"People are profit-taking on long dollar positions. CBK's mop-up and statement today helped shift sentiment on the shilling," said Julius Kiriinya, a trader at African Banking Corporation.

"If they (the central bank) come back in and banks start building up on their positions next week, the shilling could weaken towards 87.00," he added.

Traders expect the shilling to trade in the 86.00-87.00 range against the dollar, with a bias towards weakening.

"The shilling could weaken further as central bank (buying of) euros coincides with oil importers' purchases and end-year dividends being paid," said Dickson Magecha, a senior trader at Standard Chartered Bank.

UGANDA

Uganda's shilling <UGX=> is likely to stay weak amid fears of further violent political protests, although it probably will not breach the psychological 2,400 level.

Commercial banks quoted the currency at 2,389/2,393 to the dollar, a shade weaker than 2,384/2,389 a week ago, when the inauguration of President Yoweri Museveni was marred by deadly clashes between police and opposition supporters.

Spiralling fuel and food prices are adding to the volatile political atmosphere.

"I don't think it will breach 2,400," Phillip Ssali, a trader at Standard Chartered Bank Uganda, said. "The demand (for dollars) is there but the central bank has expressed interest to sell at about 2,400 so that's the factor to watch."

Traders said they saw the shilling range-bound between 2,385 and 2,395. It hit a record low of 2,424/2,429 on March 15.

The shilling has hovered near 2,400 for two weeks and traders blame the unrest, though the central bank does not. The bank sold dollars to bolster the local currency on two days last week but it made little impact.

"Demand and supply have evened out," Faisal Bukenya of Barclays Bank Uganda said. "It will stay at the same levels that it did this week" -- though analysis of the 14-day and 50-day simple moving averages suggests the shilling will stay on a weakening trend in the near term.

TANZANIA

Tanzania's shilling <TZS=> weakened on Thursday due to strong dollar demand from the oil sector and traders expect it to remain under pressure until mid-June when the agriculture export season kicks in.

Commercial banks quoted it at 1,530/1,538 to the dollar compared with 1,515/1,520 at last Thursday's close.

"The central bank has been selling dollars in the market not to support the shilling, but for liquidity purposes," said African Banking Corporation trader Gladness Deogratias.

"I don't think the shilling will reach the 1,550 level. The local currency should start to gain ground within two to three weeks when we reach the agricultural export season."

Traders said the shilling was likely to trade in the 1,520-1,530 range.

"Oil companies are importing fuel in bulk quantities against the backdrop of rising oil prices at the world market. This has triggered demand," said Msafiri Absolom, a trader at Tanzania Investment Bank.

"We expect inflows from crop exports in mid-June to stabilise the market, so the shilling will most likely appreciate in the second half of the year."

In the last week, the central bank said it traded $38.7 million on its interbank foreign exchange market.

NIGERIA

The naira <NGN=D1> is expected to fall amid strong dollar demand and a lack of local supply.

It was trading at 156.92 to the dollar on Thursday from its Wednesday close of 156.70 after the central bank failed to meet all the demand at its bi-weekly auction on Wednesday.

"There has been strong pressure on the available dollars in the interbank market as a result of tight liquidity and consistent depreciation of the naira at the official window," one dealer said.

Dealers said the bulk of the unmet demand at the official window was redirected to the interbank market, putting further pressure on the available dollars floating round Africa's biggest oil producer.

The central bank sold $300 million at 153.21 to the dollar at its auction on Wednesday, short of the $389.86 million demanded and the $499.89 million sold at 153.05 at Monday's auction.

"We expect the rate to trend up until there is large inflow of dollars from energy companies towards the end of next week," another dealer said.

Most energy firms sell dollars regularly on monthly cycle to selected banks to obtain naira to fund their local obligations.

GHANA

Pressure may continue on the Ghanaian cedi next week on the back of increasing demand for the dollar by companies.

The cedi opened this week at 1.5090 but declined to 1.5160 at the close of Wednesday's trading, mainly due to increasing demand for the greenback from companies, including the oil and gas sector, Biggles Amponsah of Access Bank Ghana said.

"The demand from corporate bodies keeps rising, even beyond the expectations of some of us," he said.

At midday Thursday, the cedi was offered against the dollar at 1.5165.

"Though there is inflow from the mining sector and from mining support service companies, the demand from the Oil & Gas sector and other importing firms outweighs the supply," he added.

Amponsah sees the pair trading within the 1.5150 and 1.5190 band next week with the greenback facing a new resistance at 1.52.

Jacob Brobbey of Barclays Bank Ghana said corporate demands for the dollar have pushed the GHS towards 1.52.

"Corporate demand is relatively firm amid a general dip in FX supply and we expect the next key resistance level of $1.5200 to hold next week," he said.

title: RPT-AFRICA  FX  WEEKAHEAD-Kenya shilling to test record low
text:
(repeats with no change to text)

NAIROBI, March 3 (Reuters) - The Kenyan, Ugandan and Tanzanian shillings are all likely to fall towards record lows next week amid strong demand for dollars from oil importers. Strong central bank intervention is not expected.

KENYA

Kenya's shilling <KES=> is seen easing towards a lifetime low due to hefty demand for dollars from oil importers, companies paying dividends abroad and the government signalling it will not intervene to prop up the currency.

Commercial banks quoted the shilling at 83.00/10 to the dollar -- 6-1/2 year lows -- compared with last Thursday's close of 82.00/10. Its lifetime low is 83.35, touched on Aug 25, 2004.

"There's a congruence of several factors working against the shilling. We have seen oil guys are really active. On top of that interest rates are really low and it's dividend season so the multinationals are repatriating," said Chris Muiga, senior trader at Kenya Commercial Bank.

"Then the Ministry of Finance comes out and says 'We're cool with the weak shilling'. When you put all this together it just points to one direction. I think the market will continue to test higher levels."

Treasury Permanent Secretary Joseph Kinyua said on Wednesday the shilling's decline was not worrying, adding that it would be good for the export sector. [nLDE7210OY]

A spike in world oil prices due to turmoil in the Middle East has also made Kenyan importers nervous.

"Oil importers have geared up for new oil consignments as they fear prices will go higher in light of the crisis in Libya," said Edwin Mathenge, a senior trader at Chase Bank.

Traders said they expect the shilling to trade in the 82.50-83.50 range. Charts suggest the shilling is in a long-term downtrend and has further to fall. [ID:nLDE71R0ZE]

TANZANIA

Tanzania's shilling <TZS=> is also expected to weaken towards a record low as companies pay dividends to offshore shareholders.

Commercial banks quoted the shilling at 1,513/1,518 to the dollar compared with 1,512/1,514 at last Thursday's close. The unit is off this week's four-month low of 1,518, a level last seen in September.

It hit a record low of 1,527 in May last year, but traders said corporate dollar demand could push it to as low as 1,540 by June.

"Many companies, especially those with shareholders outside the country, are expected to pay dividends to parent companies and thus repatriation of dollars will push the shilling further down," said National Bank of Commerce economist Yono Mtengule.

Dollar inflows from agriculture, one of the main sources of foreign currency, are unlikely to start any time soon.

"Inflows are quite limited. We expect agricultural exports such as cashew to start in April. That's when we'll see significant inflows," said Rahim Suleiman, a trader at African Banking Corporation Tanzania.

Between last Thursday and Wednesday, the central bank traded $31.15 million on its Interbank Foreign Exchange Market, statistics on its website showed.

In July to December, the central bank was the main source of foreign exchange, selling $551 million out of a total $881 million traded, according to its February monetary policy statement. [ID:nLDE7210JV]

UGANDA

Having rebounded strongly after peaceful presidential elections last month, Uganda's shilling <UGX=> is likely to fall due to weak dollar inflows and an absence of central bank intervention.

Commercial banks quoted the currency at 2,369/2,374 from last Thursday's close of 2,345/2,350. Some traders see the unit testing the key psychological level of 2,400 -- an all-time low plumbed in mid-January.

"If you look at the usual month-end demand together with an aspect of covering for dividends, I see the shilling weakening," said Lucas Ochieng, a trader at Orient Bank Uganda. "The inflows are not meeting demand."

Traders see the shilling trading in the 2,375-2,395 range into next week.

"Inflows are not healthy," said Faisal Bukenya, head of market making at Barclays Bank Uganda. "Even those who are even converting dollars are converting small amounts."

After January's record low, the central bank pledged to beef up dollar supply, although traders said it was unlikely to intervene this week.

The shilling neared a nine-day low, when it touched 2,370 on Wednesday.

ZAMBIA

The kwacha <ZMK=> is likely to firm as general dollar weakness across the G10 currencies trickles down to emerging markets. Commercial banks quoted it at 4,715 versus 4,740 a week ago.

Standard Chartered's local head of global markets Stanley Tamele said exporters had injected sizeable amounts of dollars into the market but this was being met with aggressive bids mainly from offshore banks and importers.

"The spike in oil prices above $110 per barrel has also reignited dollar demand from some oil marketing companies. The market is likely to consolidate between 4700-4800," Tamele said.

The kwacha met firm resistance around 4,600 during 2010. On the few occasions it breached that level, and went on to test but failed to breach 4,550.

GHANA

The cedi <GHS=> is likely to come under pressure due to dollar demand from manufacturers ahead of Easter and the impact of high crude oil prices.

The cedi was at 1.52 to the dollar on Thursday, weaker than 1.4950 touched on Feb. 17, and moving towards a lifetime low of 1.5790 hit a month ago.

Dollar inflows ahead of a 3-year bond auction open to foreigners accounted for much of the cedi's appreciation from those depths. Without that support, the currency was likely to weaken to 1.53, said Biggles Amponsah of Access Bank.

"These gains could not be sustained as they were highly backed by the USD inflow from the offshore investors, and not a significant improvement in economic activities," he said.

However, Databank's Sampson Akligoh said the cedi would hold its ground if the central bank stuck to its policy of regularly selling dollars.

"I am concerned about the impact of higher crude oil prices on Ghana's trade balance. This would induce depreciation pressures, which can only be contained by Bank of Ghana's participation in the market," Agligoh said. (Reporting by Kevin Mwanza, George Obulutsa, Fumbuka Ng'wanakilala, Barry Malone, Chris Mfula, Hereward Holland and Oludare Mayowa; Editing by Ron Askew)

title: UPDATE 1-Weakening Kenyan shilling not detrimental -finmin
text:
* Authorities will not intervene just yet

* Not worried because weakening is manageable

* Easing shilling good for exporters

(Adds details, quotes)

NAIROBI, March 2 (Reuters) - Kenya will not intervene in favour of the shilling <KES=> against the dollar just yet because its weakening is manageable and not destructive to business, a top Finance Ministry official said on Wednesday.

The Kenyan currency is sliding towards an all-time low and touched 83.10/20 earlier on Wednesday -- its lowest level since hitting a record low of 83.35 on Aug. 25, 2004.

"We shall not intervene just yet. We do not think the current weakening is destructive to business in terms of decision making," Joseph Kinyua, permanent secretary at the Finance Ministry, told reporters.

"I don't think we would be so much worried with manageable weakening because we still need the shilling to reflect the reality of the market, and it is good for the export business because if we take policies that are too hard, it will hurt them," he said.

Technical analysis shows the shilling has further to fall in coming weeks. [ID:nLDE71R0ZE]

Kinyua said the government wanted a competitive shilling that would support exporters too.

"If it becomes too strong it may be okay from a national pride (perspective) but not in terms of promoting prosperity and economic growth," he said.

The central bank made hard currency purchases last week, the first time it has done so this year after a series of purchases last year.

It maintains that its participation in the foreign exchange market is purely to beef up its reserves, and not intervention.

"Of course the central bank will be keeping watch of what is happening in terms of interest rates and exchange rates to ensure that they are not moving in a manner which can be destructive to economic activity," Kinyua said. title: INTERVIEW-No  intervention  planned on  Kenya  shilling -cbank
text:
* Import bill rising to $1 billion per month

* Growth for 2010 seen in 4.5-5 percent range

* Inflation seen remaining stable

WASHINGTON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - A rising Kenyan import bill is an important factor behind increased central bank dollar buying and there is no intention to intervene to influence the value of the shilling <KES=>, the head of the central bank said on Saturday.

Foreign exchange dealers have grumbled that fundamentals dictate the shilling should be stronger but that central bank purchases of foreign currency have capped its gains.

"Dollar purchases are to protect reserves and to build up reserves, not just for fun," central bank Governor Njuguna Ndung'u told Reuters on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings in Washington. "Our import bills have risen significantly to slightly over $1 billion a month, so it means that keeping four months of import cover means being in the neighborhood of $4 billion."

He said the timing of purchases was in line with the government's need to meet foreign obligations.

Kenya's foreign reserves edged up to $3.49 billion in the week to Friday [ID:nLDE6971JC]. They have risen roughly 8 percent in the past six months.

Ndung'u gave no indication as to the direction of the central bank's key interest rate. The rate was left on hold at 6.0 percent last month, and analysts said an easing cycle could end soon given inflationary pressures.

Ndung'u did not express any concern over inflation, which was steady at 3.21 percent year-on-year in September. He said there was no change to the bank's growth 2010 growth forecasts of 4.5-5 percent.

"Growth has been strengthening since towards the end of 2008 and we are going to see that (continue)," he said. "Inflation is going to remain stable." (Reporting by Matthew Tostevin; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: UPDATE 1-Kenyan shilling firms vs dollar, stocks ease
text:
* Forex investors square off ahead of weekend

* Bond trading quiet

* MPC decision positive but already priced in

* Main NSE-20 share index closes lower

(Adds market close, details)

By Richard Lough and George Obulutsa

NAIROBI, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling firmed slightly against the dollar on Friday as investors squared off positions ahead of the weekend while the main index on the Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE) eased.

At the close of trade at 1300 GMT, commercial banks quoted the shilling <KES=> at 80.90/81.00 to the dollar, compared with Thursday's close of 81.15/25, and slightly stronger than 80.95/81.05 where the currency traded earlier in the day.

"We're seeing squaring off of positions ahead of the weekend. Also, whenever it gets above 81.00 importer demand for dollars subsides," said Moses Kiboi, head of trading at Citi.

Traders said the widely expected decision by Kenya's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) to leave the central bank's benchmark lending rate steady at 6 percent sent out positive signals over the economy's health but had already been factored into prices. [ID:nLDE68M1HV]

Technical analysis showed the dollar resistance level of 80.80 with the 50-day moving average standing at 80.59.

Traders will also keep an eye on the Central Bank of Kenya, which has bought dollars in the market recently, frustrating some market players who say the shilling's fundamentals are stronger than its price.

"The central bank is still buying dollars. Anything below 81.00 is fantastic for them and we could see them picking up quite a bit," said Peter Mutuku, head of corporate desk at Bank of Africa Kenya.

Central bank said on Thursday that it does not intervene unless the market was unstable and highly volatile.

It also said that in making foreign currency purchases, it did so to meet its minimum threshold and pay for the government's external obligations. [ID:nLDE68M1RY]

Kiboi said bond trading was sluggish with most demand targeting a 2-year Treasury bond at rates between 3.75 - 4.0 percent.

Kenya accepted bids worth 13.4 billion shillings for the two-year bond at auction on Wednesday after receiving a 3 percent oversubscription. The weighted average rate was 3.698 percent. [ID:nWEA925]

On the NSE, shares in Kenyan fuel marketer KenolKobil rose to their highest since July after the firm said it expects its crude oil import licence to be re-instated following the end of a protracted dispute with the country's sole refinery. [ID:nLDE68N0C0]

The shares rose 7 percent to end at 10.10 shillings after rising 9.5 percent to 10.35 shillings in earlier on Friday.

Kenya Power and Lighting Company closed 3 percent lower at 238 shillings after its full year results failed to meet market expectations, traders said.

In earlier trade, the shares fell 10 percent to a low of 220 shillings compared with Thursday's close.

Corporate and government bonds worth 475.2 million shillings were traded at the bourse, compared with 275.9 million shillings traded on Thursday.

The main NSE-20 share index <.NSE20> closed 20.09 points lower at 4,581.72.

title: Kenya unit slides marginally as cbank buys dlrs
text:
NAIROBI, April 30 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling <KES=> softened marginally versus the dollar on Thursday as the central bank offered to buy $10 million and traders did not expect it to strengthen past the 78.50 level in coming days.

At 1100 GMT, commercial banks posted the unit at 78.65/75 per dollar compared with 78.55/65 at Wednesday's close.

"We've seen the central bank two days in a row now for monetary policy purposes," said Steve Lagat, a trader at CFC Stanbic Bank. "People are still watching to see if they keep buying."

The Central Bank of Kenya, which rarely intervenes in the market, has purchased a total $30 million since last Thursday.

"Liquidity has been tight in the money market so they are killing two birds with one stone. They have to raise reserves as well," Lagat said.

Official foreign exchange reserves have fallen far below the statutory requirement of four months import cover.

Dealers expect the shilling to face resistance at the 78.50 level.

"The shillings's ascent could be checked by the central bank's activities in the market," a report by Bank of Africa said. "The market will also keep an eye on the happenings on the political front where any negative sentiments might send the shilling tumbling."

Kenya's coalition government partners have been bickering over who should run an influential parlimentary committee, heightening tensions and fears of a return to days of turmoil.

Kenyan markets are closed on Friday to mark Labour Day.

title: E.Africa units seen in mixed trade vs dlr
text:
NAIROBI, April 29 (Reuters) - The Kenya currency is seen in choppy trade in the week to Wednesday, while the Tanzania unit is seen stronger and the Ugandan weak, all on respective central bank interventions.

KENYA:

Kenya's currency <KES=> is seen in choppy trade in the week to Wednesday on anticipated central bank dollars purchases.

At 0940 GMT, leading commercial banks posted the unit at 78.85/95 per dollar compared to last Wednesday's close of 78.40/50.

The unit had strengthened to 78.55/65 early Wednesday but ceded some ground after the Central Bank of Kenya announced that it would buy $10 million for monetary policy purposes.

"The outlook is mixed. We were expecting the speaker's ruling yesterday would give it a boost," said Friday Mwafuga, head of trading at Cooperative Bank.

The speaker of Kenya's parliament on Tuesday appointed himself the leader of the house's business committee, diffusing tension that rose in the coalition government over who should hold the position.

Despite the good news, the local unit reversed gains after the central bank's action.

Mwafuga said the regulator bought dollars either to signal that it did not want a strong shilling or to inject some local currency in a cash-strapped money market.

"The idea that they are in the market creates a bit of confusion," said Peter Mutuku, the head of corporate trading at Bank of Africa. "Because of that, we see choppy trade between 78.50 and 79.20."

TANZANIA

The Tanzania shilling <TZS=> is expected to strengthen helped by the central bank and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) selling dollars.

Commercial banks quoted the shilling at 1,328/1,338 to the dollar compared with 1,335/1,345 at last Wednesday's close. Dealers see the unit between 1,330-1,335 in coming days.

"I still feel that they (central bank) will keep on coming in, and some inflows from NGOs will strengthen the local currency," said Hamis Mwakibete, head of trading at Commercial Bank of Africa Tanzania.

The Bank of Tanzania sold the U.S. currency during the week which boosted the shilling.

"In the short term I think we will be seeing a strong shilling as long as we see this intervention," said Beven Mushambi, a dealer at Standard Chartered Bank Tanzania.

Since last Wednesday, the central bank traded $29.25 million on the Interbank Foreign Exchange Market.

UGANDA

The Uganda shilling <UGX=> is projected to trade weaker against the dollar due to a surge in demand from offshore investors and minimal inflows for the U.S. currency.

Commercial banks quoted the shilling at 2,215/2,225 per dollar compared to last Wednesday's rate of 2,180/2,190.

The shilling is expected to trade within 2,220-2,240 range in the coming days.

Dealers said the local unit hit its lowest level this month to trade at 2,225/2,250 on Tuesday prompting the central bank to intervene and sell dollars in the market to reduce volatility.

"Offshore investors are not rolling over their investment in government securities. We have seen a high number of them buying back and repatriating their dollars, which has put pressure on the shilling," said Catherine Bulinda, treasury head at Centenary bank.

Traders said end-month inflows are weak with market activity mainly driven by trade within commercial banks.

"We have not seen that much demand for dollars from the corporate clients and importers," another dealer said.

The central bank said in its monthly review that the shilling has appreciated by 5 percent in April. (Reporting by George Obulutsa in Arusha, Susan Nabadda in Kampala and Helen Nyambura-Mwaura in Nairobi; Editing by Ron Askew)

title: Kenya shilling tumbles vs dlr, market eyes c.bank
text:
NAIROBI, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling <KES=> tumbled against the dollar on Wednesday on interbank greenback purchases, touching a near four-year low as the market focused on the Central Bank of Kenya for any intervention.

At 0750 GMT, leading commercial banks posted the unit at 79.20/30 against the broadly strong dollar, compared with Tuesday's close of 78.10/20.

The 79.00 level was last seen in December 2004 and traders said the unit could close the session weaker than 79.00, barring intervention by the central bank.

The unit has weakened 8.5 percent in October as the effects of the global credit crunch spread to the east African nation.

"These are the levels around which the central bank came in last week and although the shilling still remains under pressure, guys are hesitant," a dealer with a commercial bank said.

Traders said there was light dollar demand by importers in the hope of another intervention-backed rally.

The central bank stepped in last Friday, selling an unspecified amount of dollars, according to some dealers, causing the local unit to rally.

"Importers are hoping that they will see some retracement and holding off where they can and only buying what they need to buy now," said the dealer.

Jackie Maina, an Equity Bank dealer, said fundamentals were working against the shilling due to factors such as the global crisis which analysts expect to affect the country's tourism.

The sector earned the country $1 billion last year and is just beginning to recover from the effects of a bloody post-election crisis in January and February.

title: Kenya shilling falls vs dlr on importer appetite
text:
NAIROBI, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling <KES=> eased against the dollar on Tuesday as importers, perceiving the exchange rate as favourable, flooded the market for the U.S currency.

At 0915 GMT, commercial banks posted the unit at 77.25/35 against the dollar compared to Friday's close of 76.00/20.

"There is excitement in terms of cheaper rates across the board. Many people are just seeing these as good, cheap prices and they have bought for their requirements," said Kenya Commercial Bank's Robert Aloo.

The shilling depreciated to 79.00/10 on Friday before the Central Bank of Kenyaintervened through a dollar sale, helping the unit pare some of its losses.

Aloo said there was no indication the shilling's intervention-backed rally would be sustained in the days ahead.

Bank of Africa's Kennedy Butiko said the market is watching for the central bank's next move.

"We want to see whether the central bank will come in because that is what will actually hold the shilling. Demand (for dollars) is there," he said.

Central bank governor Njuguna Ndung'u said in a statement late on Friday that there were no significant signs of foreign exchange supply constraints now or in the future.

title: Kenya shilling in slight gain, awaits direction
text:
NAIROBI, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Kenya's shilling <KES=> strengthened marginally against the dollar in quiet trade on Thursday as the market waited for clear signs on direction, dealers said.

At 0940 GMT, commercial banks posted the unit at 73.00/10 against the dollar compared to Tuesday's close of 73.15/25.

The market was closed on Wednesday due to a public holiday.

Dealers said the unit was likely to stay in a range of 72.70-73.30 against the greenback for the rest of this week.

"It is only a marginal gain and it is because of the 'new-month syndrome' whereby people expect some appreciation, assuming the traditional end-month demand (for dollars) is over," said Robert Aloo, a Kenya Commercial Bank dealer.

He said the local unit will strengthen a bit more.

"This being the first week of the month, the shilling will gain some ground and then we will go back to the same pattern of it being under pressure," he added.

The shilling has lost plenty of ground in recent weeks, due to substantial demand for the U.S. currency by diverse importers ranging from telecoms to oil firms.

Regulator Central Bank of Kenyaintervened twice last month, through sale of dollars, to stave off a slump in the currency.

"After the holiday there has not been much activity. Next week is when we will identify direction," said Solomon Alubala, the head of trading at Chase Bank. (Reporting by Duncan Miriri; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: E.Africa units seen in mixed trade in next week
text:
NAIROBI, Sept 24 (Reuters) - The Kenya and Uganda shillings are expected to weaken further against the dollar in the coming week to Wednesday, while the Tanzanian currency is expected to strengthen slightly, dealers said.

KENYA

Kenya's shilling <KES=> is expected to ease further due to increased demand for the U.S. currency, dealers said.

The local unit hit an eight month low versus the greenback last week, as the financial crisis in global markets extended to Kenya, causing volatile trade in the shilling.

To stem the shilling's fall, central bank intervened and auctioned a total of $20 million on two consecutive days. Kenya's central bank rarely intervenes in the market.

The shilling weakened to 73.45/55 at 0730 GMT from 73.00/10 at Tuesday's close. It ended last Wednesday's trade at 72.90/73.00.

"Holding other factors constant, and without any intervention by authorities, the shilling should weaken even further due to demand pressure" for dollars, a market report by Bank of Africa said.

Dealers were bearish longer term if the central bank refrained from selling more dollars.

"A weaker shilling could bring about inflationary pressures," Bank of Africa's report added.

But another dealer said the current levels would be attractive to some market players.

"This is a good level for exporters, we could see renewed interest...74 could be a ceiling for the very short term," said Noah Meely, a senior treasury manager at Citibank.

TANZANIA

The Tanzania shilling <TZS=> is seen stronger against the dollar in the coming week, helped by U.S. currency flows from the agriculture sector, donors and corporate clients selling dollars to pay shilling-denominated taxes.

Commercial banks quoted the shilling at 1,170/1,175 to the dollar, compared with 1,155/1,160 at last week's close.

Dealers said they expect it to trade in the 1,150-1,176 range in the coming week, with a bias for a stronger shilling, with dealers seeing 1,170 as resistance to further weakening for the local unit.

"Next week we expect that there will be flows from donors. Bank of Tanzania will have to sterilize these funds," Christopher Makombe, head of trading at Standard Chartered Tanzania.

"We are looking forward for inflows from the agriculture sector, mainly cashew nuts."

The shilling is also expected to gain from companies seeking to pay their quarterly taxes.

Dealers said the shilling eased during the week, undermined by banks covering their short positions, as well as buying by clients who had stayed out hoping the local unit would strengthen.

UGANDA

The Uganda shilling <UGX=> is projected to edge downwards against the greenback in the coming week, with an anticipated spike in corporate demand for the U.S. currency, dealers said.

Commercial banks in Kampala posted the local unit at 1,660/1,665 to the dollar, compared with last Wednesday's closing rate of 1,642/1,647.

The depreciation trend is expected to continue in the coming days with a trading range of 1,650-1,660.

"We are likely to see increased pressure on the local unit as corporate demand increases amid minimal inflows," said Ronald Mutebi, a dealer with Bank of Africa Uganda.

Dealers said the anticipated inflows from offshore traders looking to buy government securities did not materialise.

(Reporting by Helen Nyambura-Mwaura in Nairobi, Susan Nabadda in Kampala and George Obulutsa in Dar es Salaam; Editing by Ron Askew)

title: Kenya to revise inflation basket - stats bureau
text:
NAIROBI, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Kenya is revising the contents of its consumer prices basket and how it computes inflation, which analysts expect will shave a few percentage points off the country's spiralling rate.

The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) said it will change the CPI basket contents that were based on a household budget survey in 1993/94 to a study done over 2005/06.

In August, inflation was at 27.6 percent compared with a monthly average 9.8 percent for 2007.

The new basket reflects new consumption patterns such as mobile phone charges, bottled water and bicycle taxi fares.

KNBS will also change the method for deriving inflation to a geometric mean from an arithmetic one, KNBS officials told Reuters this week.

"For ease of comparison, there is a recommendation that worldwide, people harmonise the CPI methodology and most countries are moving to the geometric mean," said James Gatungu, KNBS's principal economist.

He said the bureau would start collecting prices in September and would not publish them for 12 months as Kenya reports inflation on a month-on-month basis. The old and new systems will run concurrently for a while, he said.

Razia Khan, Africa economist for Standard Chartered Bank, said Kenya was not doing itself any favours by having inflation that was almost twice or thrice that of neighbours already using the geometric mean.

Tanzania's inflation in August was 9.8 percent while Uganda's rose to 15.6 percent. Both border Kenya and belong to a regional customs union.

FOOD COSTS

Khan estimated the new method would probably cut inflation by more than 10 percentage points.

"Intuitively, there is some support for the idea that existing inflation is overstated. Once the new CPI index is adopted we may be looking at an inflation rate in the region of 13-15 percent," Khan told Reuters.

KNBS is reviewing the weighting for food and non-alcoholic drinks index to 50.5 percent to 40.3 percent which some critics say is intended to mask inflation amongst the poorest.

"They are trying to reduce the percentage component of food which I don't think is applicable to a lot of people," said Robert Shaw, an commentator on Kenya's economy. "Our poor will spend a bigger portion of their income on food."

Gatungu however said the study a couple of years ago showed Kenyans on average were spending less on food.

Inflation is expected to rise on impending food shortages although fuel pump prices are expected to drop, Shaw said.

Another analyst said he saw inflation falling to just below 20 percent by the end of the year, assuming decent rains and the currency not depreciating any further from current levels.

"In January, it could be significantly lower than that, down to 12-13 percent," said Stephen Bailey-Smith, Standard Bank's head of research for Africa.

The local unit sunk to eight-month lows against the dollar this week as the meltdown in international markets extended to Kenya. The central bank has however intervened by auctioning dollars in the interbank market.
